en: The Madhyamāgama (Middle-length Discourses), Scroll Upper; the fourth section is titled "The Fourfold Saṃgha," extracted from the *Dīrghāgama*.
Translated by the Western Region Śramaṇa Dharmaphala and Kang Mengxiang during the Later Han Dynasty.
Chapter One: Turning the Wheel of Dharma. **Turning the Wheel of Dharma** 1. The Turning of the Wheel of Dharma, Chapter One.
Ānanda said: "In the past, I heard this from the Buddha.

Once, the Buddha was at the Auspicious Bodhi Tree in the Victorious Way-Place (Sudharmā-maṇḍala) within the realm of Magadha. There, by the power of his virtue he subdued Māra; his awakening wisdom was divine and tranquil; his threefold penetration was unimpeded. He converted two merchants, Trapuṣa and Bhallika, granted them the Three Refuges, and having enjoined the Five Precepts upon them, they became lay devotees (upāsakas)."
In the past, there was a former Buddha named Dīpaṃkara, who prostrated himself before me and spoke my name, saying:

"In a future age, ninety-one kalpas hence, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni, and your titles shall be Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, and Bhagavat. You shall deliver sentient beings just as I do now."

"Since that time, I have cultivated my original mind through the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā), accumulating merit and practicing deeds, never wearying of the four immeasurables (catvāry apramāṇāni). My lofty conduct was extraordinary; I endured immeasurable suffering until no merit remained unfulfilled, and thus the fruit of my great vows has been realized."
The World-Honored One thought to himself:
"When I first resolved my mind, I vowed to act for the sake of all sentient beings at the request of Brahmā and Śakra; the nectar of immortality is now about to be opened—whom should it reach first?"

"In the past, when I left the household life, my route passed through the dwellings of the brahmins Ārāḍa and Udraka Rāmaputra; they received me with courtesy, and thus the two of them should come first.
Having thought this, he wished to proceed. Heaven, receiving his holy intent, spoke from the air, saying:
"Those two have been dead for seven days."
The Buddha said: "Alas!
Āḷāra and Uddaka, the nectar of immortality was about to be opened; why did you not hear it?"
The Buddha reflected again:
"The nectar of immortality shall now be opened; who is next to hear it?
Udraka Rāmaputra is next to receive this teaching."
Just as he was about to rise and depart, a deva spoke again, saying:
"This man passed away last night.
The Buddha said:

"That person suffers long-term decline; the nectar of immortality is about to open, yet they shall not be able to receive or hear it. Wandering through birth and death, by what means can this be brought to rest?
To revolve through the five realms of existence—how painful! What can be done?"
The Buddha again reflected:
"The drum of the Dharma of Ambrosia resounds throughout the trichiliocosm; who should be the first to hear it?
In the past, my father the King sent five men:"
The first was named Kūṭadanta, the second Aṭṭhaka, the third Vāseṭṭha, the fourth Dasabala-Kassapa, and the fifth Mānava-Kuṇḍika.
They provided him with oil-cake and rice and served him through arduous labor; their meritorious rewards should now be recounted.
At that time, the five men were all in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.

Then the Tathāgata first arose from beneath the tree, his marks and signs majestic and his deportment solemn; he shone brilliantly throughout the world, and his awesome spiritual power caused all who saw him to rejoice. He proceeded directly toward the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.
Before he had reached the midpoint of his journey, he encountered a brahmin named Uruvilvā.
Beholding the Buddha’s sublime and majestic presence, the brahmin was filled with a mixture of wonder and joy; he stepped down to the side of the road and cried out in praise:
"Your spiritual power moves the hearts of men, and your dignified bearing is most extraordinary. Whom did you formerly serve as a teacher that you have attained such a countenance?"
The Buddha spoke this verse for Uruvela: "The Eightfold Right Awakening is self-attained;
Free from departure and free from defilement, With craving exhausted, he has shattered the net of desire; He is self-enlightened, having received no teacher."
"In my practice, I have had no teacher or protector; my resolve was solitary and without companion.
By accumulating the single practice, I shall become a Buddha; from this, I shall penetrate the Holy Path.
Then Uḍyuka asked the Buddha:
“How does Gautama travel?
The Buddha told the brahmin:

“I wish to go to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī to beat the drum of the Dharma of Ambrosia and turn the unsurpassed wheel. Among the multitudes of sages in the three realms, none have ever turned the wheel of Dharma as I do now, leading people into Nirvāṇa!”
Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa was greatly delighted and said: "Excellent! Excellent!"
"O Gautama, as you have spoken, we pray that you open the gate of the Deathless and preach the Dharma accordingly.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata proceeded to the Deer Park, the ancient abode of seers in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, and approached those five men.

Seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, the five men consulted together, saying, "We have endured great hardship, separated from our families, and have become utterly exhausted by climbing mountains and crossing ridges—all because of this man. We thought it would be unbearable to provide him with hemp and rice."
Because Māra came to wage war against us, we hid away [these provisions].
Now he has come again; as for this single grain of sesame and single grain of rice, we are unable to endure it, yet now we have risen to seek food—how can we possibly provide it?
"I shall merely provide seats for you; let none of you kneel, rise, or exchange greetings.
If you find this unpleasant, you may surely depart of your own accord.

At that time, the World-Honored One manifested his divine powers (*ṛddhi*) for the sake of those five men. Their bodies leaped upward, and before they realized it, they paid him homage and attended upon him as they had done before.
The Buddha told the five men:
"Do not rise together in discussion; what is the meaning of performing this prostration now?
The five men all replied:
"Because of you, Siddhārtha, I have undergone further hardships; that King Śuddhodana was so violent, perverse, and contrary to the Way was entirely due to you.
The Buddha told the five men:

"Do not address the Unsurpassed, Truly Right, Tathāgata, and Perfectly Awakened One as 'you. The Unsurpassed Perfect Awakening cannot be regarded with the mindset of one still subject to birth and death."
"How can you address my father by his personal name in my presence?
He further addressed the five men:
"Observe my body; how does it compare to when I was beneath the tree?"
The five men replied to the Buddha:

"At that time you were emaciated, whereas now you are radiant again. At that time, dwelling under a tree with eyes closed and sitting upright, subsisting on only hemp and rice daily, you still said it was not the Way;
how much more so now that you have entered among people and allowed yourself physical and verbal indulgence—how can this be called the Way?"
The Buddha addressed the five men:
"In the world there are two things by which one deceives and harms oneself. What are these two?"
Those who kill and commit sexual misconduct, who rely on their power and harbor greed,
whose bodies are exhausted by extreme toil, and who lack the traces of the Path within—
these two conditions being absent, such a person is a true seeker of the Way.
One does not engage in the ninety-six arts, nor does one abandon them from afar; this is called taking the middle way, which is free from the two extremes.
What is meant by taking the middle way?

It is the attainment of awakened wisdom and practice, remaining distant from worldly knowledge, fully awakening to the six supernormal powers, and being complete in the eightfold noble path; this is called taking the middle way, dwelling in Nirvana.
When the Buddha preached this Dharma, the five men did not yet understand it.
Three went out to beg for alms while two provided offerings; for them, he spoke of the suffering of form (rūpa):
"All calamities arise from desire for form; all that is pleasing is impermanent, and persons likewise have no abiding."

It is like a magician who creates illusions by means of his intent; the foolish person becomes attached to them, coveting them without satiety, while the master of the illusion observes the transformations without defilement or attachment.
"Why is this? Because the false is not the true.
For the sake of these two people, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"When the will is dissipated in desireful conduct, the roots and growth of craving increase;
through greed for form, resentment and calamity lengthen; by leaving desire, one is free from affliction.
While three people provided offerings, two went on alms-round, and [the Buddha] spoke to them regarding the suffering of greed:
"To seek profit and pursue honor is the exclusive pursuit of the deluded and ignorant; that conduct is harmed and virtue destroyed stems entirely from greed.

In joy and anger, gain and loss, those with desire are never satisfied. These benefits are precarious and fragile, like clouds passing through a courtyard; when old age, sickness, and death arrive, nothing remains but dispersal."
"It is like a person in a dream who sees nothing upon waking; one who is wise can abandon craving and thereby attain great peace.
For these three people, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Craving is the field of the mind, Insatiable desire is the seed; The consciousness that is born from this Brings forth the harvest of suffering."
"Having severed craving and abandoned the pursuit of gain, there shall be no further sorrow of coming and going.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One extensively expounded the Dharma with its various divisions; the five men immediately attained understanding and requested to become his disciples.
The Buddha said, "Welcome, bhikṣu!"
They all became śramaṇas.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"There are two things in practice that lead to falling into extremes: [the extreme of indulgence and the extreme of self-mortification]."
First, their thoughts dwell on form and desire, lacking pure resolve;
second, they rely on and cling to craving, unable to purify their conduct and resolve.
These two matters cause them to fall back into extreme practices, leading to rebirths where they do not encounter a Buddha and remain far removed from the true Path.
If one can sever craving and diligently cultivate clarity, one may attain nirvāṇa.
What is meant by nirvāṇa?
It is first knowing the Four Noble Truths.
What are these four? First is suffering; second is its origin; third is its cessation; and fourth is the path leading to its cessation.
Thus, bhikṣu, by subsequently maintaining awakened wisdom and practicing dhyāna with a single-minded focus, you shall receive the retribution of the Way, and your Dharma-eye will become clear.
By understanding those Four Noble Truths, one gradually enters the path.
What is meant by suffering?

It is the suffering of birth, the suffering of old age, the suffering of illness, the suffering of death, the suffering of grief, lamentation, pain, and despair, the suffering of separation from what is loved, the suffering of encountering what is hated, and the suffering of failing to obtain what one seeks; furthermore, it is because the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are intensely clung to that they constitute suffering.
What is meant by "clinging"?
Clinging to what is beloved, and clinging even to what is not beloved.
What is meant by "cessation"?
Regarding all that is cherished, one realizes its cessation; by neither loving nor dwelling upon it, one realizes that it is entirely exhausted.
What is called "entering the Path"?
The Eightfold Right Path is the truth.

First is right view, second is right resolve, third is right speech, fourth is right action, fifth is right livelihood, sixth is right effort, seventh is right mindfulness, and eighth is right concentration.
This is the origin of suffering; by its cessation, one enters the Path.

This is the Noble Truth of non-arising: that which does not arise does not age; that which does not age does not fall ill; that which does not fall ill does not die; that which does not die is without pain; and that which is without pain is supreme auspiciousness, tending toward Nirvāṇa.
At that time, the Tathāgata spoke in verse:
“The Ultimate Way has no coming or going; It is profound, subtle, pure, and wondrously true.
Neither perishing nor being born again— This state is Nirvāṇa.”
"This essential tranquility is unsurpassed; having exhausted what was done, one creates nothing new.
Though there be excellent realms in the heavens, none can compare to Nirvāṇa.
When he had spoken these words, the five companions, including Kauṇḍinya, attained the Dharma-eye.
The Buddha asked Kūṭadanta,
"Do you understand?
Kūṭadanta withdrew from his seat and replied:
"Not yet awakened.
The World-Honored One again addressed Kūṭadanta:
"In the distant past, there was a king named Caṇḍapradyota who, accompanied by various court ladies, entered the mountains for recreation."
The King ordered his officials to halt at the foot of the mountain, while he followed only his female attendants as they trekked to the summit.

The King, utterly exhausted, lay down to rest; meanwhile, the women left him to gather flowers and saw a practitioner sitting upright beneath a tree. Delighted in their hearts, the women all approached and paid him homage.
The practitioner offered a prayer of blessing, asking, "Sisters, where have you come from? He then bade them take their seats and preached the Dharma for them.
When the king awoke and sought his courtesans, he found them sitting before that practitioner.
The king was by nature jealous and malicious; an evil thought arose within him, and he asked the practitioner, "For what reason have you enticed another's courtesan and seated her here? Who are you?"
The practitioner, foreseeing that the king’s mind would surely give rise to violent malice, replied:
"I am a person of patience.
The king drew his sword from its scabbard, lopped off both of his arms, and asked:
"Who is it? He replied, "It is truly a person of forbearance."
He further cut off his ears and nose, yet his mind remained firm and unmoved; he was still called a person of forbearance.
Seeing that the practitioner’s countenance did not change, the king came forward and repented his transgression.
The practitioner told the king:

"Because of your lust for a woman's beauty, you have now cut my body with a blade; yet I endure it as the earth does. Once I have surely attained equal and perfect enlightenment, I shall use all-encompassing great wisdom to sever your cycle of birth and death."
The king, realizing his offense was grave and that he would surely suffer heavy retribution, prostrated himself on the ground, entreating mercy and forgiveness.
The practitioner told the king:
"I am truly one who practices patience; my blood shall turn to milk, and the severed parts shall be restored."
Immediately, as he had spoken, milk flowed forth and his physical form was restored.
Seeing this proof of his forbearance, the king hoped for his certain salvation and again expressed his feelings:
"If you truly achieve the Way, I pray that you will deliver me first."
The practitioner replied, "It may be so.
The king’s delusion ceased; he took his leave and returned to the palace.
The Buddha told Kūṭadanta:
"The man of the Way who practiced patience at that time was I myself;
King Duḥṣanta was you, Kūṭadanta."
"Do you understand,
Kūṭadanta? Kūṭadanta withdrew from his seat and addressed the Buddha:
"Excellent understanding!
World-Honored One!
When this Dharma was spoken, the five companions, including Kauṇḍinya, were freed from outflows and their minds were liberated; they all attained arhatship.
Furthermore, eighty thousand deities from the heavens above attained the Dharma-eye.
The trichiliocosm shook with a great trembling.

This was the Tathāgata’s first turning of the unsurpassed Wheel of Dharma at Vārāṇasī for that which had not yet been turned; he brought great deliverance to all, and there were none who did not joyfully accept it.

Chapter Two: Manifesting Transformations (alternatively titled "Welcome") At that time, in the city of Vārāṇasī, there was an elder named Ajita who had a son named Nāga (in the language of Jin, "Precious Renown"), who was twenty-four years old.
He was called Shengqimiao (Born Wondrous). He possessed lapis lazuli sandals that grew upon his feet as he wore them.
His parents held him in high esteem and regarded him as extraordinary, giving him the name Baocheng (Jewel-Appellation).

They constructed separate dwellings for him so that he might change his quarters according to the cold and heat; they provided him with the entertainment of singing girls, day and night without ceasing.

In the middle of the night, Ratnayaśas suddenly awoke and saw that all the female entertainers were like corpses, with pus and blood overflowing and their limbs severed and broken. The rooms and all the furnishings appeared like a cemetery. Startled, he ran toward the door, which opened of its own accord. Heaven and earth were pitch black, and he saw only a small light; he hurried toward the eastern city gate, which also opened by itself. Its radiance illuminated the Deer Park, and following the light, he went to the Buddha. Beholding his physical marks and signs—majestic and resplendent—his fear ceased and his delusion was resolved.
Raising his voice, he sighed and said:
"For a long time I have remained in the prison of affection and craving, bound by the shackles of name and form; now that I hasten toward the World-Honored One, shall I truly attain liberation?"
The Buddha said, “Young man, welcome! You have awakened well! This place is free from sorrow;
all conditioned activities have reached their ultimate end. He then prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the stainless Dharma-eye; withdrawing from his seat, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to become a disciple.
The Buddha said:
"Welcome, bhikṣu! and he immediately became a śramaṇa.

At dawn the next day, the women did not see the snake; they searched everywhere in a state of panic, sobbing and weeping together. The mistress was struck with alarm and wonder, and asked them about the circumstances of what had happened.
He replied, "I do not know where Baocheng is now.
Terrified and trembling, the elder immediately dispatched horsemen to search in all directions; the father mounted his son’s carriage and hurried out to seek him.

On his way, he came across a body of water named Vārāṇasī. Having crossed the water, he saw his son’s jeweled sandals left upon the bank; he then followed the footprints and proceeded directly to the Deer Park.
The Buddha, through his skillful means, caused the father and son not to see one another.
When the elder saw the Buddha’s majestic appearance and his excellent physical marks, joy and fear arose within him simultaneously; forgetting to pay his respects, he asked the Buddha:
"My son, Ratnaghoṣa, has come this way; have you, Gautama, seen him?"
The Buddha told the elder,
"If your son were here, why would you worry about not seeing him?
The Buddha then preached the Dharma for him:
"Birth and death arise from ignorance; there is separation from those one loves. Having destroyed two billion evils, one enters the stage of Srotāpanna.
Upon hearing this, Ratnayaśas attained liberation of mind and immediately became an Arhat.
When father and son met, their affection was slight; the elder was filled with joy and, withdrawing to sit at one side, addressed the Buddha:
"Today my heart is glad.
My feelings hold two joys: [text missing]"
"First is the joy of meeting the Buddha and attaining understanding; second is the blissful joy of being free from craving.

At that time, four friends of Ratnayaśas—named Pūrṇa, Vimala, Kātyāyana, and Sūta—hearing that Ratnayaśas had already become a śramaṇa, were filled with wonder and joy such that their hair stood on end, and they said:
"This man’s virtue is lofty and his enlightened influence shakes the realm; we all turn to him in devotion.
Now that he has become a śramaṇa, his Way must surely be true, for it has caused this man to suddenly renounce glory and profit."
Together they went out to visit the Buddha and also to see Baocheng; they then proceeded as one.
Upon seeing the majesty of the Buddha, they were moved by their original vows and, with hearts filled with joy, immediately attained understanding and prostrated themselves in worship.
He then addressed the World-Honored One, saying:

"I have long been parched with the thirst for the Way and transformed by its teachings, my mind having been empty and receptive for many days. Do not consider me base or unworthy; I pray that you will accept me as a disciple.
The Buddha said:
"Welcome, bhikṣus! At these words,
they all became śramaṇas.
He expounded for them the fundamental nature of the mind, explaining that its essence is pure; upon hearing this meaning and understanding it with their minds, they immediately attained arhatship.
At that time, in a district near Vārāṇasī named Tuṣa, there were fifty men who, on some business, had come to the kingdom.
Hearing that Ratnākara, Pūrṇa, and the others had all become śramaṇas, they each thought to themselves:

"These sons of wealthy families were accustomed to luxury and indulgence, yet their talents surpassed those of the world; now they have all been moved by the influence of the Way. Gautama must be divine, for he has caused these noblemen to no longer look back upon worldly glory."
Each of them conceived the thought of wishing to go to the Buddha.

They immediately departed together and went straight to the Deer Park; as their original vows required that they be delivered, upon seeing the Buddha they attained understanding and wished to become his disciples.
The Buddha said, "Welcome, bhikṣu!"
They all became śramaṇas.
Following their original intent, they swiftly accomplished the essentials of the Dharma; with defilements removed and bonds severed, they all attained arhatship.
At that time, in the midst of the Deer Park, there was a great assembly engaged in feasting, singing, and dancing.
At that time, there was a woman of extraordinary beauty who danced amidst the assembly; everyone rejoiced with boundless delight.
Before her dance had even concluded, she suddenly vanished, leaving the crowd bereft of their joy and filled with sorrowful anxiety.
Then, appearing again at a distance of a hundred paces from them, the great assembly rushed forward; the woman led them to the Buddha and suddenly vanished.
The people asked the Buddha, "A certain woman was dancing here just now; did you see her, Gautama?"
The Buddha told the assembly: "Observe your own bodies first; what is the use of observing others?
Form and desire are impermanent; there is meeting and there is separation. They are like bubbles and foam; the foolish are attached to them, and from this attachment, calamities arise."
"The body is a vessel of suffering; all sentient beings are likewise so.
When the great assembly understood this in their hearts, they wished to become śramaṇas.
The Buddha conferred the precepts upon them all, manifested the Path of the True Truths, and they all attained arhatship.
The Buddha commanded the bhikṣus:

"Go each of you separately to extensively deliver sentient beings; according to the Dharma you perceive, act as guides and bridges, universally bestow the Dharma-eye, proclaim the Triple Gem, uproot craving and eliminate existence, and lead them to enter Nirvāṇa."
"I shall now go alone to the district of Uruvilvā.
The bhikṣus received these instructions, prostrated themselves with their heads at his feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and then departed.
Chapter Three: The Conversion of Kāśyapa. Thereupon, the Tathāgata returned to the realm of Magadha, arrived at the district of Uruvilvā, and stayed for the evening in the Sṇa Garden of a brahmin.
At dawn the next morning, he took his alms bowl and went to the gate of Sñāya. The Buddha manifested a golden light that illuminated the interior of the hall.

The two daughters of the Brahmin—the elder named Nanda and the younger named Nandabalā—saw the light and were filled with joy; they immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated themselves, and invited him to enter.
The Tathāgata ascended the hall and instructed the two daughters; they took refuge in the Triple Gem and received the five precepts.
The World-Honored One then said:
"The body does not belong to oneself; all things return to emptiness."
The two men understood the meaning in their hearts and received it with reverence upon their heads.
The World-Honored One thought to himself:
"I originally set out to study because I wished to deliver sentient beings; now the Māra of the Desire Realm has submitted to my transformative teaching."

Near the banks of the Nerañjarā River lived a brahmin of the Kāśyapa clan named Uruvilvā; he was one hundred and twenty years old, his fame was far-reaching, and he was revered by the people of the world. He maintained a fire sacrifice, never flagging day or night.
He had five hundred disciples who were fond of learning.
Kāśyapa’s two younger brothers followed their elder brother as their masters, believing him to have attained the Way.
Each of them had their own disciples, all of whom resided downstream.
Kāśyapa thought to himself:

"My reputation is lofty and the people of the kingdom look up to me with devotion; yet my skills are shallow and easily exhausted. Once exhausted, my fame will decline. I must devise a sound strategy to preserve the nation's great expectations."
He then went to search for the dragon and, using his arts, summoned it. He built a meditation chamber for it and instructed the dragon, saying:
"If anyone should rashly enter this chamber, you must breathe fire and emit poison to extinguish them."
Whenever the dragon arrived at a festival, it would never fail to set fire [to the offerings].
Far and near, everyone said:
"The Great Master’s Way is divine."
Because of this, Kāśyapa’s fame and merit flourished.
The World-Honored One thought to himself:
"In the past, when I left the household life, I encountered Uruvilvākāśyapa on the road; we made a vow that once the Way was perfected, he would be the first to deliver me."
"For the sake of all beings, I shall indeed grant this.
Yet, when I now observe the hearts of the people, they are all focused upon Kāśyapa; it will not be possible to turn them back.

It is like a tree with beautiful fruit that is too high to reach; there is no way to eat the fruit except by cutting the roots of the tree and lopping off the branches—the fruit can certainly be obtained only in this way!"
"All that is feared resides within the dragon.
If I first subdue it, Kāśyapa will follow!
Only then will the Great Way transform beings without limit."
The Tathāgata said:
"When the sun shines upon the world, its virtues are threefold:
first, its radiance dispels the darkness so that nothing remains unclear."
The second is the depiction of various forms in five colors, narrating their appearances;
the third is the sprouting of buds, wherein the essence of all things flourishes.
The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world likewise has these three aspects:
First is all-encompassing great wisdom, which illuminates and dispels the darkness of ignorance;
second is the classification of the five destinies, explaining the origins of speech and action;
third is the salvation through expedient wisdom, benefiting and bringing peace to others.
Having thought thus, the World-Honored One rose from this Śāla grove and set out toward Kāśyapa at dusk.
Before he had reached his destination, he manifested a golden radiance, such that the trees, earth, stones, and soil all took on a golden hue.
A disciple of Kāśyapa was carrying a jar to fetch water when he beheld the transformation; his heart was moved, and filled with wonder, he looked around.
Seeing from afar the World-Honored One, whose brilliance illuminated the world, he did not recognize what marvel it was and ran back to inform his teacher.

The master and his disciples all came forth; the World-Honored One’s majestic spiritual power and brilliant ceremonial splendor were so magnificent that Kāśyapa was struck with trepidation and, in his state of bewilderment, failed to comprehend it. He then thought to himself:
"If this is indeed the Buddha, my eyes have finally attained their goal!"
"This must be a celestial being, for his eyes are twitching again!
Later, Si reflected and understood, saying:
"Could this not be Prince Śuddhodana’s son, Siddhārtha?"
"I have calculated through the cycles of destiny:
'The Prince of Śuddhodana possesses the merit to correspond with a Holy King; he will not delight in glorious rank, but shall surely attain Buddhahood.
Previously I heard that he has left the household life—has his Way been perfected?"
The Tathāgata suddenly arrived, and Kāśyapa was greatly delighted, saying:
"Welcome, Gautama! I hope you have been well and at ease.
The Buddha then spoke in verse for Kāśyapa:
"Observing the precepts brings peace until old age; faith and uprightness lead to a virtuous dwelling;
wisdom is the supreme protection for the body; and not committing any evil is peace.
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha:
"I only pray that you will condescend to honor me by accepting this simple meal.
The Buddha replied to Kāśyapa:

"The Dharma of the Buddhas of antiquity does not involve eating after midday. However, I wish to clarify my sincere intention regarding one matter; I hope you will not be parsimonious with your time."
Kāśyapa replied, “I regret that I have made no prior preparations; I merely sit here with a humble mind, revering your virtue.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"I wish to request a night's lodging; would you be so kind as to grant me your hospitality?
Kāśyapa replied to the Buddha, "In our tradition as brahmins, we do not sleep in the same room. I beg your forgiveness for my lack of generosity."
"What is this great life?
The Buddha pointed to the chamber of tranquility and asked, "And what is this chamber?"
Kāśyapa replied, "There is a divine dragon within who is impetuous and malevolent; whenever anyone enters the room, he invariably spits fire to burn and harm them."
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa, "Lend this to me. Kāśyapa replied:
"In truth, there is no love [of gain] here; I fear only that the dragon will cause harm.
The five hundred disciples were cowed and held their breath in terror, fearing that the Master would grant his permission to the Buddha.
They entreated him for a third time; Kāśyapa remained hesitant, feeling that while he had no intention of disobeying, he feared certain calamity.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa, "I have already extinguished the fires of desire within the three realms; the dragon shall not harm me! Kāśyapa replied:
“The venerable Gautama may dwell here as he pleases.
He then exercised his majestic spiritual power and entered the chamber.
The five hundred disciples, believing that the dragon would cause harm, all wept with tears, lamenting: “What a pity! This noble person will be harmed by the dragon.”
After the Buddha had sat for a short while, the dragon emerged from its cave and spat venom, coiling around the Buddha; the Tathāgata transformed the venom so that it all became flowers.
Seeing his venom turned into flowers encircling the Buddha, the dragon’s rage intensified and he spat forth fire, thinking he could thereby cause harm.

The hot vapors returned to the dragon, who was so stifled and oppressed that he felt as if he were dying. He raised his head and beheld the Buddha; recognizing the Honored One, a cool breeze rushed toward the dragon. Seeking relief, he approached the Buddha; the fire was extinguished and the poison removed, and he took refuge and entered the almsbowl.
Thereupon the Tathāgata manifested a blaze of fire, brilliant and reaching to the heavens.
Kāśyapa’s disciples rose directly to observe; seeing the Buddha’s radiance, they thought it was the fire of the dragon and cried out in lamentation:
"What a pity! This True Man has ultimately been struck by the dragon's calamity."
Kāśyapa and his disciples were startled and fled together; the five hundred disciples cried out in unison to rebuke their teacher:

"Since the opening of heaven and earth, we have never seen a human being as wondrous as Gautama—so venerable and noble! We regret that we did not observe him closely; by what cause shall we see him again?"
Shedding tears and wiping his eyes, he uttered this verse:
“His countenance shines with the luster of purple-gold; His face is full and his hair is deep blue-black.
A Great Man endowed with a hundred merits, His divine and wondrous features accord with the *Lakṣaṇavyañjana-sūtra*.”
His square body stood sixteen feet tall, adorned with the eighty marks of excellence;
the light from his crown illuminated the deepest darkness—how swift was this sudden impermanence!
Later disciples, believing that fire had harmed the Buddha, wailed and lamented in profound grief.
"If Gautama has been harmed, what would be the use of my life?
He leaped into the fire, which became cool and temperate; looking back, he said to his teacher, "Gautama is unharmed!"
"What we previously called 'dragon-fire' was, in fact, surely the Buddha's radiance!
The master and his disciples were in a state of agitation, holding their breath until dawn arrived.
At early morning, the Tathāgata emerged from his chamber carrying his alms bowl; Kāśyapa was overjoyed and said:
“Does the Great Wayman still exist?
What is within the vessel?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"As for the so-called venomous dragon, he has already been subdued and has received the Dharma.
The five hundred disciples all declared that the Buddha was divine.
Kāśyapa, though inwardly humbled, was stingy with his reputation and remained somewhat arrogant, saying:
“The Great Way-man is truly divine.
Even so, he is not yet like me, who have already attained Arhatship!
Kāśyapa addressed the Buddha:
"I pray that the Great Way-man will remain here; I wish to provide you with offerings.
The next morning, he prepared a meal and went in person to invite the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Go now; I shall follow shortly after.

Just as Kāśyapa had returned, in the time it takes a person to bend and extend their arm, the Buddha traveled eastward to Pūrvavideha, several hundred billion *li* away, where he took the fruit of the *jambū* tree, filled his alms bowl, and returned.
Before Kāśyapa had even arrived, the Buddha was already seated upon his bed.
Kāśyapa asked the Buddha,
"Great Way-man, by which path have you come?"
The Buddha said, “After you had departed, I went east to Pūrvavideha and took these fruits called jambu, which are fragrant, delicious, and fit for eating.
After the Buddha had finished his meal and departed, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"Although the Great Way practitioner is divine, he is still not as true to the Way as I am.
At the time of the next meal, [the king] again went to invite the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"You may go; I shall follow shortly. Kāśyapa turned back.
The Buddha traveled south to the furthest limit of Jambudvīpa, where he gathered *kharjūra* dates, filling his bowl to the brim, and returned.
Before Kāśyapa had even arrived, the Buddha was already seated upon his bed.
Kāśyapa asked the Buddha,
"For what reason have you arrived first?"
The Buddha said, "Go south and take these fine fruits; they can be used to cure your illness.
After the Buddha had eaten and departed, Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa is truly divine and truly wondrous.
The next day, Kāśyapa again went to invite the Buddha, and the Buddha said,
"I shall follow you there shortly."
The Buddha went west to Aparagoyānī, took *āmala* fruits, filled his bowl with them, and returned.
Before Kāśyapa had arrived, the Buddha was already seated upon the couch.
Kāśyapa asked the Buddha:
"From which direction have you come?
He replied, "I went west to Aparagoyānī to fetch āmalaka fruits; you may eat them."
After the Buddha had finished his meal and departed, Kāśyapa thought again:
"The deeds performed by this Great Śramaṇa are truly miraculous.
The next day, Kāśyapa went once more to invite the Buddha, and the Buddha said:
"I have just now arrived following behind.
Kāśyapa looked back, but suddenly the Buddha was no longer there;
the Buddha had already gone to Uttarakuru in the north and taken naturally grown non-glutinous rice.
Before Kāśyapa had even arrived, the Buddha was already seated upon his couch.
Kāśyapa asked the Buddha,
"From where have you come?"
The Buddha replied, “Go north to Uttarakuru and take some of this non-glutinous rice; you may eat it.
After the Buddha had finished his meal and departed, Kāśyapa thought to himself alone:
"This Great Way-man is so divinely wondrous!

On the following day at mealtime, the Buddha took his bowl and went to the man's house himself; having taken the rice and returned, he wished to rinse his mouth after eating but found no water. Śakra, Lord of the Devas, immediately descended and pointed to the ground with his finger, whereupon a pond was naturally formed.
At the time of the afternoon, Kāśyapa was wandering about when he saw a pond; finding it strange, he asked the Buddha, "By what cause has this come to be?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:

"I obtained your food this morning, but when I wished to rinse my mouth, there was no water. The Lord of Devas pointed at the ground, which turned into a pool for my use; this pool should be named 'The Pool Created by Pointing' (Aṅgīrasa).
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This Great Wayman is divine and wondrous! His merit is immeasurable!"
On a later day, the World-Honored One moved closer to Kāśyapa and sat beneath a tree.
During the first watch of the night, the Four Heavenly Kings descended together to listen to the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma; the radiance of the four kings was as bright as a blazing fire.
Kāśyapa rose during the night and saw four fires before the Buddha.
At dawn, he asked the Buddha,
"Does the Great Wayman also serve fire?"
The Buddha said, "No.
Last night the Four Heavenly Kings came to listen to the Dharma; it was their radiance."
Kāśyapa thought again:
"This great śramaṇa possesses supreme spiritual power, for he has even brought these devas here.
Nevertheless, his way is still not as true as my own."
On the second day, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, came at night to listen to the Dharma; Śakra’s radiance was twice that of the Four Great Kings.
Kāśyapa rose in the night and, seeing the light before the Buddha, thought to himself:
"The Buddha must still be worshipping the fire."
At dawn, he asked the Buddha,
"Have you not tended the sacrificial fire?
Its brightness is twice that of last night."
The Buddha said, "It was the light of Śakra, who descended to listen to and receive the Dharma.
Later in the night, the seventh Brahmā heaven also descended to hear the Dharma; the radiance of that Brahmā was twice that of Śakra.
When Kāśyapa saw the light, he suspected that the Buddha was performing fire rituals.
At dawn, he asked the Buddha,
"The Great Wayfarer must surely be attending to the sacred fires."
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"It was the light of the seventh Brahmā Heaven, who came last night to listen to the Dharma.
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa possesses such majestic power that he has moved the heavens and caused the Brahmā gods to descend.
Kāśyapa’s five hundred disciples each tended three fires, totaling fifteen hundred fires in all.
At dawn the next morning, he lit it, but the fire would not burn at all.
Finding this strange, he informed his teacher.
The teacher said:
"This must surely be the work of the Buddha," he thought.
He hurried off to inform the Buddha:
"My five hundred disciples lit fires this morning, yet they simply would not ignite. Is this the work of the Buddha?"
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa,
"Do you wish for it to burn?
He asked this up to three times, and [Kāśyapa] replied:
"I wish to make it burn.
The Buddha said, "You may go; the fire shall burn."
At his voice, they all burst into flame.
Kāśyapa thought again:
"This Great Way-man is so supremely divine!"
Kāśyapa himself tended three fires; when he attempted to extinguish them the following morning after lighting them, they would not go out.
His five hundred disciples and those who assisted him tried to extinguish them together, but they could not be extinguished at all.
Suspecting it was the Buddha’s doing, he went to inform the Buddha:
"I have been tending my three fires, yet they cannot be extinguished.
The Buddha said:
"Do you wish for it to be extinguished? He replied,
"I truly do wish for it to be extinguished."
The Buddha said,
"The fire may now be extinguished.
As soon as he spoke, it was immediately extinguished.
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This Great Way-man is supremely divine and most wondrous; everything he does is harmonious.
On a later day, Kāśyapa’s five hundred disciples were out chopping wood when each of them raised their axes but could not bring them down. Alarmed, they went to inform their teacher.
The teacher said,
"This was done by that great śramaṇa.
He then went at once to inform the Buddha.
"My disciples were just now splitting firewood together, but the axe was raised and could not be brought down.
The Buddha said, "Go; the axe shall come down."
He immediately lowered it and was able to use it.
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"This great śramaṇa is indeed miraculous!"
On a later day, the Buddha returned to the foot of the tree and saw the discarded, worn-out garment; he thought of washing it.
Śakra, Lord of the Devas, perceiving the Buddha’s noble intention, went to Mount Pāṇḍava, took a square stone and a hexagonal stone, and provided them for the purpose of washing and drying the cloth.
As Kāśyapa was walking about for observation, he saw two stones by the side of a pond;
finding them strange, he asked the Buddha, "These two stones by the side of the pond are exquisite and fine; from where did they emerge?"
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"I wish to wash my robes and shall need to dry them; the Lord of Devas has sent this stone for me to use.
Kāśyapa thought again:
“Gautama’s divine virtue moves all to emotion.

After the Buddha had entered the Indradvīpa pool to bathe, as he was about to emerge, there was nothing for him to grasp. Above the pool was a tree named Kāśmarī, which was exceedingly large and beautiful; the tree bent down toward the Buddha, and the Buddha pulled himself out of the pool by it.
Kāśyapa saw that the tree was bent down and, finding it strange, questioned the Buddha about it.
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"This morning I entered the pond and was about to emerge from the water when the tree spirit lowered its branches so that I might pull myself out."
Kāśyapa thought again:
"This Great Way-man possesses such profound virtue that it moves the great tree to bend down.
Desiring to ensure that Kāśyapa would certainly submit, the Buddha then entered the Nairañjanā River.

The water was deep and swift; by his supernatural power, the Buddha cut off the flow and caused it to stand still, rising above the heads of the people and churning up dust from the bottom, through which he walked.
When Kāśyapa saw the Buddha enter the water, fearing he might drown, he immediately took his disciples and boarded a boat to rescue him.
Seeing that the water had parted and dust was rising from beneath it, he beheld the Buddha and rejoiced greatly, exclaiming:
"The Great Way-maker still lives!"
He asked again:
"Do you wish to board the boat?
The Buddha said:
"Let it be raised. The Buddha thought to himself that he should pierce the bottom of the boat so that no trace of leakage would remain.
Kāśyapa was greatly astonished:
"This great śramaṇa! His wondrous transformations are beyond naming.
At that time, the king, officials, and people of Magadha went to Kāśyapa to pay their respects during the annual festival, enjoying themselves for seven days.
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
"The Buddha’s virtue is holy and sublime; if the multitude were to see him, they would surely reject and abandon me.
It would be well if he were not to appear for seven days."
The Buddha, knowing his intention, remained hidden for seven days.
When the dawn of the eighth day arrived, Kāśyapa thought again:
"Now that there is still food remaining, it would be a joy to offer it to the Buddha!"
Just as he thought this, [the Buddha] suddenly arrived.
Kāśyapa was greatly delighted and said:
"I had just been thinking that I wished to make an offering to you; how wonderful it is that you have come so promptly!"
"Where has he been lately?
From where does he come now?
The Buddha told Kāśyapa:
"You thought to yourself:
'The Buddha’s virtue is holy and brilliant; if the multitude were to see him, they would surely reject and abandon me.
It would be a joy indeed if he did not appear for seven days.'"
"Therefore, I remained hidden.
Because you now think of me, I have come again.
Kāśyapa thought to himself:
“The Buddha is truly supreme and divine; he truly knows the thoughts of men.
Having known that Kāśyapa’s mind was already subdued, the Buddha addressed him:
“You are not an Arhat, nor do you know the true Way. Why do you engage in such falsehood, claiming for yourself such nobility?”

Thereupon Kāśyapa’s heart was struck with alarm and his hair stood on end; realizing that he himself possessed no Way, he immediately prostrated himself and said, “The Great Way-man is truly divine and sagely; you even know the thoughts within my mind.”
"Would it not be possible for me to receive the transformation of the divine from a Great Way person and to receive the sutras and precepts,
becoming a śramaṇa? The Buddha said, "Excellent!"
"Announce this to your disciples:
'You are the National Preceptor; now that you have entered the dharma-robes, how could you know this alone?
Kāśyapa received these instructions and, looking back at his disciples, said:
"I have now witnessed your divine transformations together with you; I have attained faith and understanding, and I shall become a śramaṇa.
Where will you all go?
The five hundred disciples replied in unison:
"Whatever we know is entirely due to the grace of our Great Master; whatever the Master honors and trusts in, we wish to follow accordingly.
Thereupon, the master and his disciples went together to the Buddha, prostrated themselves, and said:
"We all possess the intent of faith; we pray to become your disciples."
The Buddha said, "Welcome, bhikṣu!"
They all became śramaṇas.
Kāśyapa discarded his fur robes, water jar, staff, sandals, and all his implements for tending the sacrificial fires into the water.
At that time, Kāśyapa’s two younger brothers—
The next was Nadi-Kāśyapa, and the youngest was Gayā-Kāśyapa; each had two hundred and fifty disciples, and their dwellings were situated in rows along the riverbank.
Seeing the robes, belongings, and fire-offering implements of the various brahmins drifting downstream, the two younger brothers were struck with alarm;
fearing that their elder brother and his disciples had been harmed by others, they immediately followed their own followers and traveled upriver.
Seeing that his elder brother and his disciples had all become śramaṇas, he asked in wonder:
"My elder brother is advanced in years and possesses profound wisdom; he is revered by both the king and the subjects. In my mind, I considered my brother to have attained arhatship."
"To abandon the way of a brahmin and instead study the dharma of a śramaṇa—this is no small matter.
Is the Buddha’s way so venerable that its virtue alone is so exalted? Kāśyapa replied:
“The Buddha-way is most supreme; its Dharma is immeasurable. Although we have studied under him for generations, none among us has ever attained the divine wisdom of the Way like that of the Buddha!
Hearing this, the two younger brothers each said to their disciples, “We wish to follow our elder brother; where will you go?”
The five hundred disciples raised their voices together, saying:
"We pray to become like our Great Master.
They all immediately prostrated themselves, seeking ordination as śramaṇas.
The Buddha said, "Welcome, bhikṣu!"
They all became śramaṇas.
Then the Tathāgata, together with a saṃgha of one thousand bhikṣus, went to the great grove of Kāśyapa trees and sat down, entering into samādhi.

Suddenly disappearing, he came from the east and vanished beneath a tree; the same occurred in the four directions. He leaped up and stayed suspended in mid-air without falling, emitting water and fire from his body, ascending and descending at will.
The bhikṣus looked up with joy, unaware that the Tathāgata had returned to his original seat; none among them realized it.
The bhikṣus were filled with delight, went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew from their seats, and addressed the Buddha:
“What is the name of this manifestation?”
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"This is called the manifestation of supernormal power (ṛddhiprātihārya).
Furthermore, there is the manifestation of instruction; listen attentively, bhikṣus."

The functioning of mind, intellect, and consciousness, through the causes and conditions of defiled attachment, is decisively rectified and categorized; this is called the manifestation of instruction.
Furthermore, there is the manifestation of the teaching of the Dharma, which bhikṣus should contemplate with earnest attention.
Attachment to physical form is decline; that which is cherished by the six sense-faculties is decline. When decline does not cease, suffering arises.
What is meant by the arising of suffering?
The fires of lust, anger, and delusion ignite, giving rise to pain and itching, as well as the fears of old age, sickness, and death.
"This is what is meant by the manifestation of teaching the Dharma.
When the Buddha had thus turned the wheel of the Dharma three times, at that moment a thousand bhikṣus, their outflows exhausted and their expectations severed, all attained arhatship.
The Buddha spoke these verses for the bhikṣus:
"Now these thousand bhikṣus, Elders of venerable virtue,
Having abandoned error and cultivated right view, Enter the meditative wisdom of non-conceptualization."
When this Dharma was being taught, the devas, nāgas, and spirits all delighted in hearing it.
Chapter Four: Converting King Bimbisāra. At that time, the World-Honored One desired to go to Rājagṛha to convert the sovereign and his subjects.

On that very day, the King of Rājagṛha dispatched a messenger to attend upon the Buddha with his command, to pay his respects with the utmost reverence, and after the prostrations were completed, to present these words:
"The Lord of the Nation, Bimbisāra, bows his head before you!"
Recently, we have learned that the World-Honored One has perfected the Way and is now titled Buddha; gods, humans, and all other classes of beings rejoice and rely upon this fortunate era.

We humbly beseech the World-Honored One to bring forth benefit and peace, and pray that you will extend your protective nurture and grace our humble kingdom. Craving your holy transformation, we wait with empty hearts and overflowing joy; may you take pity on the multitudes and cause them to attain liberation.
The Buddha commanded the bhikṣus:
"Prepare yourselves quickly; you shall go to the king's invitation.
Having received these instructions, the bhikṣus completed their preparations and followed him in attendance.
The messenger galloped back to report:
"The World-Honored One has looked upon us and, leading a community of a thousand bhikṣus, is now staying beneath the Śūrpāraka tree, forty li from the city."
The king then consulted the late king’s final instructions:
“If the Buddha enters the kingdom, you must personally go out to welcome him; those who welcome him shall obtain immeasurable merit.

He immediately ordered a thousand chariots, ten thousand horses, and seven thousand attendants to be prepared. Once the preparations were complete, he ascended his carriage and departed the palace, heading toward the city.
The city gates closed of their own accord, and both the chariots and horses stumbled; the king was greatly terrified and feared a great calamity, thinking:
"My sins are grave! That such a disaster has occurred."
A voice from the sky said:
"The person for whom the King made his former vow is now imprisoned; because he vowed to be linked with him, this has caused the gates to close.
Thereupon, a general amnesty was proclaimed and the prisoners were released.
The gates opened of their own accord, allowing him to reach the Buddha’s dwelling.
Seeing from afar the Tathāgata’s exquisite marks and radiant light, the king immediately descended from his chariot and dismounted to unsheathe his sword.
The Buddha knew that King Bimbisāra was by nature arrogant, haughty, and conceited, and wished to cause him to understand quickly by transforming the ceremonial protocol of the king’s attendants.

If King Bimbisāra were to look at his attendants and see that they were no different from himself, he might fear that the Buddha would not recognize him; thus, he prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated him three times to the right, and having finished his salutation, he declared:
"I am Bimbisāra, the King of Magadha."
Thus it was repeated three times.
The Buddha said to the king:
"I perceive your mind; how could I perceive only your physical form?"
Bimbisāra was greatly delighted and immediately withdrew to take his seat.

The ministers and commoners each paid their respects; among them were those who performed prostrations, those who announced their names, and those who simply bowed; having completed their salutations, they withdrew and stood back.
The Buddha commanded him to sit; having received the instruction, he took his seat.
The Buddha addressed King Bimbisāra:

"By virtue of merit accumulated in past lives, you have become a king; now that merit is further increased, it shall cause the people within your kingdom’s borders to be loyal and filial, wealthy and joyful, free from sorrow and protected by blessings. Possessing virtue and auspiciousness, there shall be nothing that is not beneficial."
The assembly harbored doubts:
"Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa is renowned for his long-standing reputation; now that he is together with the Buddha, who should serve as the teacher?
The Buddha, perceiving the thoughts of the assembly, addressed Kāśyapa:
"If there are those who kill living beings to perform sacrifices, hoping thereby to obtain blessings—
can they truly attain them?
If one enters the mountains to seek the Way without a teacher, can one attain the Way?"
Kāśyapa said to the Buddha:
“Sacrificing living beings for worship does not yield merit;
the celestial deities do not eat them, and the one who kills incurs sin.”
"If one studies the Way without a teacher, the Way will ultimately not be accomplished. Kāśyapa said to the Buddha:

"In the past, I served the fire-gods, never flagging day or night, practicing with diligent hardship for many years. I had five hundred disciples who were fond of these arts; they maintained the fires with vigor, avoiding neither cold nor heat. My age was advanced and my faculties matured, yet I never attained even a semblance of realization. I merely passed on the delusions of my predecessors to later generations, claiming this to be the Way; it was a fruitless toil with no reward."
"Now that I have received the Buddha's teaching and washed away the defilements of my mind, I have already attained arhatship.
The Buddha said to Kāśyapa,
"Manifest your arhat’s supernormal powers."
Kāśyapa, having received the command, immediately entered a state of meditative concentration; his body rose into the air several *zhang* above the ground.
From the waist upward there was fire, and from the waist downward there was water;
then again, from the waist upward there was water, and from the waist downward there was fire, raining water upon the flames so that his robes remained dry and did not soften.
Abiding in emptiness, he manifested transformations, appearing and disappearing seven times; from his body he emitted light, brilliant in five colors.
Flying from the east, he vanished before the Buddha’s seat; in the four directions, above, and below, his manifestations were likewise.
Having completed his transformation, he joined his palms, knelt with long knees, and addressed the Buddha:

“I, the disciple Kāśyapa, have received the compassionate grace of the Buddha and am liberated from the bonds of sin. The Tathāgata is uniquely venerable; I receive him at the crown of my head as the sovereign of the three realms.”
The Buddha spoke in verse for Kāśyapa:
"If a person lives for a hundred years, Worshipping fire and practicing heterodox arts,
It is not equal to honoring the sublime Truth, Which illuminates all things."
"If a person lives for a hundred years, learning what is false and with an unwholesome mind,
it is not as good as living for a single day, diligently receiving the True Dharma.
The king and his ministers then realized that Kāśyapa was a disciple of the Buddha.
The Buddha told Bimbisāra:
"The eyes of the people in the world do not merely perceive forms;
suffering and pleasure are impermanent, and the body cannot endure for long."
The minds of people in the world mostly harbor evil and little goodness.
Their thoughts are manifold, and they seek only to gratify their own desires; yet, if one can renounce this disposition, one may attain the Way and achieve merit equal to that of Kāśyapa.
Do not, on account of your nobility and wealth, indulge your passions at will;
do not, on account of your power and autonomy, harbor insatiable greed and lust;
do not, on account of your strength and dominance, oppress and欺凌 the weak.
Do not, out of anger, wrongfully kill those who are innocent.
Do not follow the mind of lust, do not follow the mind of greed, and do not follow the mind of wrath.
Cease evil and promote good; faithfully uphold the true words.

One should constantly reflect upon the severity of death and the intensity of the sufferings of old age and sickness; by contemplating one's conduct in this way, one may likewise attain the supernormal powers of Kāśyapa.
When the eyes behold forms, the mind should suppress them so as to remain unmoved by the beautiful or the ugly.
When hearing various sounds with the ears, the mind should maintain restraint, remaining free from both joy and anger.
When smelling fragrances or stenches with the nose, the mind should exercise self-mastery, ensuring that the emotions remain unattached.
When the mouth craves various flavors, the mind should maintain its integrity, contemplating that no [defiled] thoughts arise.
When the body encounters objects of touch, the mind should exercise restraint, ensuring that consciousness does not become entangled in frivolity.
The five aggregates come from without; their restraint depends on the mind. The six sense organs have no master, and the decaying aggregates have no name.
Kāśyapa’s merit lies simply in cultivating them thus.
In human life, having received this physical form, there is much anxiety, suffering, and affliction:
hunger, thirst, cold, and heat; the foolish reckon these to be pleasures, while the wise perceive them as suffering.

Wives, children, honors, and profits—worldly people are deluded by these things; yet all such matters inevitably disperse, for even a thousand or ten thousand years must ultimately return to extinction.
The Buddha spoke in verse for Bimbisāra:
"One who acts as a leader of the world, Following what is right without being crooked,
Compassionately guiding others and demonstrating propriety— Such a one is a Dharma King."
"Abounding in compassion, virtuous, forgiving, and upright; kind, loving, and delighting in benefiting others;
having benefited them with impartiality—in such a way, the multitude will gather around and be close to him.
Thus the Buddha told Bimbisāra:
“How many years has it been since Your Majesty built this palace?
The King turned to a minister beside him, and the minister replied,
“It has been seven or eight hundred years since the palace was constructed.”
The Buddha asked the ministers,
"In total, how many kings have there been?
The ministers immediately replied:
"More than twenty kings.
The Buddha asked Bimbisāra:
"Do you recognize all these kings?"
Bimbisāra replied, "I know only my father; I do not know my ancestors.
The Buddha said to Bimbisāra:
"Only the earth is permanent; human beings are impermanent.
Those who love their own bodies ought not to harm life, nor ought they to slander those who possess the Way."
The birth and death of sentient beings all arise from affectionate attachment.
Parents say of themselves:
"These are those whom I have given birth to; these are my children."
"A son is not produced by his father and mother; rather, it is because one has maintained the precepts in their entirety in a previous life that one attains birth as a human being.
Those who commit evil deeds fall into the hells, the animal realm, or the realm of hungry ghosts after death; this results from what they themselves have done and does not arise through another."
"Sin and merit are clear and manifest; Your Majesty should reflect deeply upon this!
The Buddha said to the king:
"If a child in the womb were blind or deaf, would the mother know it beforehand?"
The King replied to the Buddha,
“Indeed, I did not know beforehand.
The Buddha said:
"This child's present state is due to the karmic retribution of his past lives; it is not the fault of his parents.
While the child was in the womb, even if he were sagely and wise, his mother could not have known it beforehand."
All this arises from practicing purity; it is not due to the power of one's parents.
This principle is clearly proven—Your Majesty, consider it well!
When people commit offenses, their actions fall into three categories:
Speech that wounds others, physical conduct that is violent and harmful, and a mind solely intent on envy and jealousy—
if one can restrain these three, although one may not yet attain Nirvana, one will enjoy noble status and freedom among gods and humans.

It originates in the human essence; from delusion comes form, from form arises emotion, from emotion arises consciousness, from consciousness arises desire, and from desire come father and son. From father and son arises affection, and from affection arise grief and sorrow, revolving through the five realms of existence without ceasing.
People likewise do not know from whence they come when born,
nor where they go when they die;
unaware of their own root, they merely address one another by name.
Is this the father?
Is this the son?
Only those who have attained the Way can know their origin.
“Birth and death arise from causes and conditions, fundamentally originating from ignorance; all things are impermanent.
Great King, uphold this!
Thus the Buddha told Bimbisāra.

“If there are virtuous people in the kingdom who are prudent, compliant, loyal, and filial; upright, pure, respectful, and yielding; whose talents are broad and whose wisdom is far-reaching; and who do not violate the king’s laws—though they may not originally belong to the noble class, why does Your Majesty treat them differently?”
The King replied to the Buddha,
"Those whose names and reputations are prominent and who are chosen for their capability shall be granted office.
The Buddha said to the Great King:
“The Way and its Dharma have no partiality; they assist only those who are good.
One who upholds the five precepts is called a lay follower of pure faith (*upāsaka*).

Through diligent and direct entry, seeing the Truth and not turning back, one attains the stages of *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, and *arhat*—each according to their original mind, with the stages of the Way following in succession.”
When the Buddha had spoken these words, twelve thousand people from the king and the nation, as well as eighty thousand devas, all attained the fruit of the Path.
The Buddha said to Bimbisāra:

"The King has been traveling for a long time; since the palace is distant, please return early. Your oxen, horses, and attendants will become weary from standing still. On a later day, I shall go to the city myself."
The King rose, paid homage to the Buddha, received the precepts, and withdrew.
His ministers and officials followed suit, joyfully coming forward to receive the precepts.

While the King and his ministers were receiving the five precepts, all within and without, including the horses, became silent and still. The various Brahmins, moved by transformation, submitted their hearts and all came forward to receive the precepts, withdrawing with great joy.
Once the King had ascended the chariot, the ministers knelt and offered their congratulations:
"O Great King, by your merit!
You have encountered the appearance of a Buddha in the world, and have further caused us, your subjects, to bathe in pure transformation."
King Bimbisāra returned to the palace and issued a command that all within the inner court observe the fast and uphold the precepts.
All throughout the kingdom believed, understood, and rejoiced.
Then, Śakra, Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, scattered flowers over the Buddha. At that time, among those seated in the assembly, there was a prominent elder named Kalandaka.
He thought to himself:
"It is a pity that I have given my garden to the Nirgranthas.
The Buddha will surely arrive first; I shall offer it to the Buddha and the Saṃgha, regretting my previous gift and wishing to abandon it forever."
The elder was so sincere in his devotion that he could not rest even upon his mat; his past merits followed him, and his virtuous fortune deserved to be complete.

A great ghost general named Bhaṣa, receiving the divine intent of the Buddha and knowing the elder’s thoughts, immediately summoned yakṣas to drive away the Nirgranthas—shameless, naked heretics who ought not to remain here.
The master of spirits, having received the imperial decree, beat the Nirgranthas and dragged away their implements.
The Nirgranthas were terrified and fled, crying out,
"What kind of evil person is this?"
"To cause such violent harm!
The master of spirits replied,
"The elder Kalandaka shall take possession of the Bamboo Grove and construct a vihāra for the Buddha."
"The Great General Bhaṇḍika merely saw the imperial decree ordering you to be driven out.
The next day, the Nirgranthas went together to the householder and severely rebuked him for his reasons:
"Why have you changed the object of your charity?"
"This has caused those like us to fall into exhaustion.
Not having expected that the Elder would be so distressed, Kalandaka was filled with joy, thinking:
"My wish is fulfilled!"
"The Buddha’s holy and vast radiance shines upon me with utmost sincerity.
He then replied to the Nirgranthas:
"These masters of ghosts are violent and full of malice; fearing they will surely cause harm, it would be better to abandon them and seek safety elsewhere."
The Nirgrantha, filled with resentment, departed in anger that very day.

The elder was overjoyed; he constructed a vihāra, monastic cells, and seating arrangements, completing all the preparations. He then went to the site of the Śirīṣa tree shrine and invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
The World-Honored One accepted their offerings and stayed there; at that time, his great transformation brought universal salvation, and there were none who did not rejoice.

Chapter Five: Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana Come to Study. The Buddha was staying at the Bamboo Grove Monastery in Rājagṛha, together with a great assembly of one thousand bhikṣus, all of whom had attained arhatship, such as Upatiṣya and others.
He had a minister named Nārada.

There was also a brahmin named Śāriputra who had perfected his cultivation of ascetic practices and welcomed those who came to study; he had two hundred and fifty disciples who were fond of the way of the immortals.
Among his disciples, there were two preeminent followers whose talents were difficult to equal:

the first was named Upatiṣya, and the second was called Kauṇḍinya. Their brilliance and wisdom were profound and far-reaching; they investigated the principles until they mastered the subtle and the minute.
Śāriputra fell ill and, knowing his end was near, addressed the two worthies:
"These newly initiated students set their wills upon the practice of the Way; I have burdened you both, and you must ensure they fulfill their aspirations."
The two men respectfully agreed, received the instruction, and set out to practice it.
At that time, the World-Honored One commanded the bhikṣu Aṭṭhaka:
"Go forth to propagate the teaching; wherever you go, there will surely be those to be saved."
As for those who may be seen, their wisdom is far-reaching and clear; apart from the Tathāgata himself, none can engage them in debate.
If you encounter them, speak directly of the fundamental nature of dharmas; do not engage in reciprocal banter, lest you invite their derision.
Having received the command, Aśvajit adjusted his robes, took up his bowl, and paid obeisance to the Buddha before departing.

At that time, Upatiṣya was wandering about with his disciples for sightseeing when he saw Aśvajita from afar; his deportment was so composed and elegant that it was unlike anything he had ever heard of or seen—what kind of Dharma practitioner could this be?
"Regarding the alteration of dress and customs, we must inquire about what is appropriate.
The two men went forward together and met on the road; they then asked Ai-bie, "Your robes and insignia are contrary to the norm; from where do they originate?"
"How could there be a teacher of such renown from whom we might hear [the Dharma]?
At that time, Aṭṭhaka replied in verse:
"My years are yet young, And my days of study are still but shallow."
How could one proclaim the ultimate truth, The vast and great meaning of the Tathāgata?
The source of all dharmas Is empty of causes and conditions and has no master.
One who quiets the mind and reaches the fundamental source Is therefore called a śramaṇa.
Upatiṣya, having heard the meaning of the Dharma, contemplated its ultimate principle and reflected to himself:

"I have been fond of learning since childhood; from the age of eight I followed a teacher until I was sixteen, when there were no writings on the arts of the ancient seers that I had not mastered. Throughout the sixteen great kingdoms, I was regarded as one of vast erudition, yet I had never heard such a teaching of essential truth.
Now, while wandering for pleasure, I have encountered this treasure; the subtlety of these words is sweeter than ambrosia."
His mind awakened and his intellect liberated, he immediately attained the Dharma-eye; returning to the monastery, he was filled with immeasurable joy.
Seeing his countenance so radiant with delight, Kauṣṭhila suspected that he had attained the Deathless (Amṛta).
He then asked Upatiṣya:
"Have you obtained the Ambrosia?
Do not fail your original vow; let us share a small portion of its benefit."
Upatiṣya recounted the verses he had heard to Kolita; upon hearing them once, he did not understand, but after they were recited a second time, he did.
Reflecting on them repeatedly, he too attained the Dharma-eye.
The two deliberated, saying:

"The ambrosia of our original vow has now been obtained for us to taste; how could we not go together to the place of the Great Śramaṇa, and at that oceanic abyss, bathe ourselves in purity and refinement?"
Their deliberations were in harmony and their hearts were one; they made elaborate preparations for their departure. Kūṭadanta thought to himself:
"When my teacher was approaching his end, he entrusted me to his disciples, charging me to bring them to completion.
To now abandon them is contrary to the principles of righteousness and leaves me ill at ease."
He then addressed his disciples:
"That Great Śramaṇa possesses the immortal transformation of ambrosia; he has torn asunder the mundane net and practices the tranquil conduct of one whose mind is stilled.
I wish to request instruction from him to exhaust the subtle and return to the truth."
"Where will you go? The disciple replied,
"That I am now able to see and hear is due to the grace of my Great Master."
The Great Man is revered by all; receiving this command, we leap with joy, craving and admiring the nectar of immortality, and wish to follow behind you.
Master and disciples, our wills being in harmony, immediately departed from their dwelling and proceeded to the Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Now there are two worthies who, together with their disciples, following the practice of their original vows, desire to become śramaṇas."
"It was the power of Aṅgada that brought this achievement to completion!
The bhikṣus received the instruction and looked out expectantly for their assembly.

Upatiṣya, Kolita, and the others saw from afar the Tathāgata’s marks and signs radiating with brilliant light; their spirits were moved and their hearts trembled, and they sighed to themselves, saying:
"How fortunate that I have lived this life to receive your pure instructions! Its glory is beyond words!
He stepped forward to sit before [the Buddha] and prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha's feet.
Having completed his prostrations, he was filled with boundless joy and delight; after a brief moment, he approached and spoke these words of sincere emotion:

"Having been submerged in the abyss of various transgressions and worldly evils until this very day, I now turn back from the secular world to reach the ultimate source; I pray that you will grant me acceptance so that I may take my place among the ranks of the Sangha."
He immediately granted permission; their hair fell away of its own accord, and they both became śramaṇas.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"These two men had made a vow before the Buddhas of the past to wait until my Way was perfected so that they might attend upon me and serve at my side."
The Buddha said to Upatiṣya, "Your lofty title is merely flowery and lacks substance; restore your original name, Śāriputra.
Kaulita, restore your name to Mahāmaudgalyāyana."
"Because he attained Arhatship through this very teaching, the Buddha commanded his attendant:
'The ancient thousand bhikṣus shall receive the formal precepts this evening; you must not go elsewhere.'"
That very night, they conducted a count by tally-sticks and found there were one thousand two hundred and fifty people.
When the Buddha had finished establishing the precepts, the bhikṣus were filled with joy; all were solemn and reverent, and they paid homage to the Buddha before withdrawing.

Chapter Six: Returning to the Father’s Kingdom. Now, the Tathāgata was about to return to the Śākya kingdom, accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus—all of whom had attained arhatship, whose spirits were tranquil and who possessed subtle supernatural penetrations, and who clearly understood the origins of the conduct of sentient beings throughout the three periods of time—namely, the Venerable Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Uruvilvākāśyapa, Nadīkāśyapa, Gayākāśyapa, and others, numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty persons.
At that time, King Śuddhodana of Kapilavastu dispatched the brahmin Udayin to visit the Bamboo Grove and invite the Buddha to return to his kingdom.
Upon seeing the Buddha’s marks and signs, which radiated brilliance throughout heaven and earth, Udayin felt a profound joy in his five senses.
He prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, then withdrew to stand to one side. With a composed mind, he knelt upright and addressed the Buddha:
“Your father, the King, sends his distant greetings to Siddhārtha. Hearing that you have attained the Way and are again delivering all beings, yet I alone have not received your grace.”
"I was originally intended to return, and for that reason I have now sent this messenger.
The Buddha asked Udāyin:
"Is my father, the King, at ease in his daily life?"
Udāyin said to the Buddha, “The Great King is in good health; he thinks only of the World-Honored One.
The Buddha told Udāyin:
"Do you delight in this path?
Udāyin replied, "I do indeed delight in it."
“World-Honored One!
The Buddha accepted Udāyin, ordaining him as a śramaṇa and conferring upon him the Dharma precepts.
Udāyin thought to himself:
"Now that I am a disciple, there is no further cause for me to return;
Your Majesty must await news—by whom shall I report back?
The Buddha, knowing Udayin’s thoughts, desired to turn back and proceed.
"Udāyin! Do not associate with worldly affairs or remain attached to your former home.
Udāyin addressed the Buddha:
“Will the Buddha return to the country of Śrāvastī?
The Buddha said,
“I shall return.”
Having received the command, Udāyin withdrew and knelt before the Buddha, asking:
"I wonder on what day you will arrive?
The Buddha told Udāyin:
"In seven days from now, he will surely arrive at Śrāvastī.
Udāyin was filled with joy, prostrated before the Buddha, and departed.
Thereupon, Udāyin returned to Śrāvastī and went to the palace to request an audience.
The gatekeeper reported,
"Udāyin has returned and is at the gate seeking an audience.
The King ordered him to be questioned.
"I long for Udāyin as one who thirsts for a drink; why do you delay so long before announcing your arrival?
He pushed back those who were supposed to sit, repeating this three times, and only then did he step forward.
When the King saw that Udāyin had already donned the dharma robes,
he asked Udāyin, "Have you become a śramaṇa? Udāyin replied:
"To serve the Buddha's Dharma.
The King asked Udāyin:

"When Siddhārtha was in the palace, he was uniquely intimate with you; you entered and exited and moved about with him without having to report anything. Now that he has sent you back, how could he have gone outside to the gate to seek admission on his own?"
Udāyin replied to the king:
"The Buddha teaches bhikṣus not to be intimate with laypeople or to long for their homes, because the monastic and the secular are distinct.
The king asked Udāyin:
"When my son was in the palace, his clothing was of the finest quality;
now that he has set out on the Way, what clothes does he wear?
Udāyin pointed to his robes and said:
"His attire was such as this!
The King immediately shed tears and said,
"When Siddhārtha was at home, I built a palace for him, carved with the seven treasures and the most exquisite jewels in the world."
"Regarding this current dwelling, how does it compare to my own?
Udāyin replied to the king,
"I always dwell beneath a tree."
"For all Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, the Way and its Dharma are thus.
The King asked Udāyin:
"When my son was in the palace, he had mats and cushions, fine rugs and silks, all soft and delicate;"
"What kind of things are used for sitting mats now?
Udāyin replied to the king:
"We use grass for our sitting mats; this simple purity serves to eliminate greed."
The king asked Udāyin:
