"When Siddhārtha was at home, I provided him with a kitchen of every kind of sweet, fatty, and exquisite delicacy; what, then, does he now eat?"

Udāyin replied, "When the time comes, I shall take my bowl and go to bring blessings to sentient beings; whether the food be coarse or fine, I shall offer prayers of blessing for the donor's household.
Upon hearing these words, the king again shed tears.
The King asked Udāyin:
"When Siddhārtha was asleep, I wished to awaken him; only after I plucked the strings of my lute and sang could he be roused.
Now that he is in the deep mountains, by what means shall he be awakened?"
Udāyin replied to the king,
"The Tathāgata’s samādhi has neither day nor night.
The king asked Udāyin:
"When my son was in the palace, for his ablutions he used eight kinds of fragrant juices;
for his ablutions now, what things does he use?
Udāyin replied to the king:
"The eight liberations are pure water, used to wash away the defilements of the mind.
The King asked Udāyin:
"When Siddhārtha was in the kingdom, sandalwood and *suhaka* were used to anoint his body; [how is it now?]"
"Now that you have set out for the Way, what things do you possess?
Udāyin replied to the king:
"The categories of virtue, concentration, and wisdom perfume the eight difficult states."
The King asked Udāyin:
"When Siddhārtha was at home, I had four kinds of exquisite jewels fashioned for his bed;
what materials are used for that upon which he sits now?"
Udaya replied, "The four dhyānas are my bed; I have stilled my mind and am free from desire.
The king asked Udaya:
"When my son was in the palace, he was guarded and attended by a multitude of officers; who now are his attendants?
Udāyin replied to the king:
“The disciples who train in the Way are called the Bhikṣu-saṃgha; they attend upon the World-Honored One, numbering one thousand two hundred and fifty people in all.
The King asked Udāyin:
“When Siddhārtha was at home, if he went out on excursions, there were four kinds of vehicles—oxen, sheep, elephants, and horses—to serve as mounts.”
Regarding your current departure, what vehicle do you ride?
Udāyin replied to the king:
“The Four Noble Truths and the supernormal powers are my carriage; I travel by flying upon them.”
The King asked Udāyin:
"When my son went out for excursions, he was adorned with banners, standards, and feathered streamers;
what now are these fluttering flags?"
Udāyin replied, "The fourfold kindness and compassion extensively adorn all living beings.
The King asked Udāyin:
"Whenever Siddhārtha went out, bells were struck and drums were beaten, and spectators filled the roads;
now that he wanders and dwells here, what sounds are there?
Udāyin replied to the king:
"When the Buddha first attained the Way, he went to the kingdom of Vārāṇasī and struck the drum of the Dharma of Ambrosia; the five Kauravas attained arhatship.

Eighty thousand devas all entered the stages of the Path, and among the ninety-six types of heterodox sects, there were none who did not rejoice and submit. The unsurpassed sound of the Dharma resounded throughout the trichiliocosm."
The king asked Udāyin,
"Which kingdom does Siddhārtha now wish to govern?
Udāyin replied to the king:

“The realm governed by the World-Honored One is beyond measure; he instructs all sentient beings, and there are none who do not receive deliverance. With an impartial mind, he universally rescues them, without partiality toward any place.”
The King asked Udāyin:

"When my son was in the kingdom, he contemplated the exposition of righteous governance and assisted me in bringing peace to the people; his every action conformed to ritual propriety, and none failed to follow his influence.
Now that he dwells alone, what does he contemplate?"
Udāyin replied to the king:
"The World-Honored One contemplates emptiness; suffering and pleasure are not real. That which exists returns to extinction; the spirit is tranquil and non-active.
Upon hearing these words, the king said:
“Catastrophe! Siddhārtha, everything exists; why do you say it does not?
You have turned against us, Siddhārtha, and become an enemy to men!
Udāyin said to the King:
"Even if wise men were to fill the world,

and each person had a hundred heads, each head a hundred tongues, and each tongue could explain a hundred meanings— if one were to combine the voices of all these people to praise the Tathāgata for an entire kalpa, they would still fail to proclaim his virtues; how much less so what I have said,
which does not equal even one ten-millionth part of them."
"Only between Buddha and Buddha are their virtues fully manifest.
The King said: "Excellent!"
"Will the Buddha come?
On what day will he arrive? Udāyin replied:
"He shall arrive in seven days.
The King was greatly delighted and immediately commanded his ministers:
"I shall go forth to welcome the Buddha."
The ceremonial procession of attendants followed the regulations for the entry and exit of a sage-king.

The roads were leveled and smoothed, and the ground was sprinkled with fragrant liquid; banners and streamers were erected throughout the streets and alleys of the city. All the preparations and decorations were most fitting, and the distance for the chariots, horses, and retinue was limited to forty *li*.

On that day, the World-Honored One rose from the Bamboo Grove together with a community of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus; moved by his majestic spiritual power, the devas attended him as he entered Śrāvastī for the first time.
The route passed through a body of water named Aruṇa;
having crossed the water to the bank, he used his supernormal powers to investigate and clearly perceived that Devadatta’s evil intent had arisen within him, making him difficult to transform.
He then manifested his supernormal powers to inspire faith and submission in them.
He ascended into the air to a height of seven *ren* above the ground; though his feet seemed to tread upon the earth, he was actually in mid-air.
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
"Behold those carriages and horses, resplendent in five colors; they resemble the chariots of the Heavenly Emperor when he goes forth on an excursion.

At that time, the multitude saw the Buddha and the Sangha treading upon the ground, yet when they looked up at the footprints, they were seen suspended in mid-air. As the procession gradually descended from above until it reached the welcoming ranks, its height was level with the heads of the people; thus, even those who were stubborn and unyielding bowed their heads in submission, taking refuge and paying homage.
Only Devadatta alone gave rise to an evil thought:
"My son has gone forth to study the Way, yet he merely performs illusory arts to delude people in this manner.
I too shall perform arts once more to widely convert the masses."

Thereupon, the Father King, seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, was moved by a convergence of both love and reverence—first, his respect for the Way, and second, his affection for his son. He immediately descended from his elephant chariot, unfastened his sword, and set aside his parasol. With tears streaming down, he approached the Buddha, bowed his head at the Buddha’s feet, and praised him with these verses:
“Born through the conditions of merit and virtue, With the thirty-two auspicious marks;
The trees lean as I bow my head in reverence, Now that the Way is perfected, I pay three prostrations.”
Thereupon, the Father King questioned the Buddha with these verses:
"When my son was formerly in my house, He rode upon elephants and chariots named 'Jewels';
Now his feet tread upon the ground— How can he endure such suffering?"
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"The chariot and horse of birth and death—how can this perilous vehicle endure for long?
Harnessing the five supernormal powers to gallop forth, there is no limit to where one may go."
Originally you wore robes of the seven precious gems, rare, exquisite, and most elegant;
now, with shaven heads and clad in hempen garments, how can you feel no shame?
To wear shame as one's clothing—worldly clothes only increase dust and grime.
The Dharma robe is the garment of the True Man; one who has stilled the mind is named Tathāgata.
Originally you used vessels of gold and silver, and the various flavors were most fragrant and delicious;
now you practice begging for food—how can such coarse and wretched fare be swallowed?
The flavor of the Dharma is the food of the Path; hunger and thirst are now eliminated.
Out of compassion for the world, I go forth to beg; holding my bowl, I bring merit to sentient beings.
Formerly dwelling in a separate palace, attended by a multitude of court ladies and guards, I now wander alone.
Dwelling alone among the mountains and trees, how could one not feel fear?
Having eliminated the terrors of birth and death, you have now entered into primordial non-being;
free from thoughts of sorrow or joy, your abode is called the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
When I was formerly in my own home, I bathed with fragrant perfumes;
now dwelling among the trees of the mountains, what thing shall wash away the impurities of the body?
The treasury of the Way serves as my bathing pool, its depths filled with the water of rectitude.
"Having bathed, the three poisons are exhausted; the Threefold Knowledge is swift and peerless.
Thereupon, the Father King invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha to come to the Royal Garden to establish it permanently as a vihāra.
The Buddha accepted the King’s intention and entered the vihāra, where he sat beneath a nyagrodha tree and extensively expounded the teachings for seven days without ceasing.

Those who listened were filled with joy; among them, some resolved to follow the Mahāyāna, some delighted in the practice of the pratyekabuddhas, some conceived the aspiration for arhatship, and some became śramaṇas—each according to their resolve, attaining results in accordance with their practice.
The women within the city each gave rise to wholesome thoughts, weeping with grief and reproaching themselves:
"Now that the World-Honored One has returned to our kingdom, it is by the merit of the men that they alone have been able to see the Buddha;
we, obscured by our own transgressions, have not partaken of the flavor of the Dharma—why do we suffer so?"
The Buddha, knowing all the thoughts in his mother’s mind, praised her, saying:
“Excellent! You have conceived a virtuous resolve and desire to hear the Dharma; you shall truly attain liberation from suffering.”
The Buddha then said to the king:

"The arising of the Dharma is difficult to encounter, and the Way of the Teacher is difficult to obtain. You should issue an edict throughout the kingdom for all women who delight in hearing the Dharma to come forth and listen to its reception."
The king immediately issued a proclamation, saying, "Those who wish to see the Buddha are permitted.
All the women within the city were filled with joy and came forth together; they approached the Buddha to pay their respects and then withdrew to stand aside.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma according to their needs; each understood it and attained the Dharma-eye.
The king, his ministers, and the people, filled with joy, paid homage to the Buddha and withdrew.
At that time, the bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
"Within the kingdom of the Śākyas, men and women, old and young, having heard the Buddha preach the Dharma, each obtained a resolution according to their own thoughts;
yet the King, our father, listened to both [the teaching and the responses], so why do you not record what he has attained?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"The father king’s affection has not yet ceased; as father and son they treat one another, their hearts of reverence are not yet complete. For this reason, it cannot be granted.
The following morning, the Tathāgata took only Maudgalyāyana with him and went to the royal palace, where he ascended the hall and sat.
The Buddha commanded Maudgalyāyana:
"Manifest your power of the Way.

Receiving these instructions, Maudgalyāyana ascended into the void; he appeared and vanished seven times, emitting water and fire from his body. Descending from above, he came forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to attend upon him on the left.

When the father-king beheld this transformation, his mind was liberated and filled with joy; his worldly attachment was severed, and a heart of reverence arose within him. Rising to bow before the Buddha, he said:
"Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"If the merit of a disciple is already such as this, the majestic virtue of the Tathāgata is difficult to measure!
Thereupon, he resolved his mind upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path.

At that time, whenever the father-king visited the Buddha’s dwelling, he observed that the bodies of the thousand followers such as Kāśyapa were exceedingly unsightly; every time, his mind was dissatisfied, thinking:

"Although these bhikṣus are refined in spirit, they lack outward appearance. I should urge those of my own clan who delight in non-action to become śramaṇas, selecting only those who are upright and handsome."
He immediately ordered his kinsmen:
"Tomorrow there will be an assembly in the palace; you must arrive as soon as you receive this command.
The King then addressed his royal relatives, saying:
"Āyuṣmān Āśvalāyana read my marks and said:

'If the Buddha does not leave the household life, he shall become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin Rāja), ruling over the four continents; his attendants and retinue shall all be upright and handsome.'"

"Now my disciples lack exemplary appearance; I now wish to betroth and welcome those who possess the Way and have sufficient dignified bearing, so as to complete the number of the Sangha and bring glory to the World-Honored One."
They all said, "Excellent!
We shall listen and be delighted; we beg leave to withdraw and prepare ourselves, and shall depart in seven days.
Devadatta then informed the attendants:
"We are the sons of kings; now, having renounced worldly glory, we have left home to dwell in the Way. Our attire is refined and represents the pinnacle of worldly excellence.
On that day we set out with solemnity, elephants, horses, and carriages worth tens of thousands of gold pieces, while onlookers lined the roads."

Devadatta’s crown and turban fell naturally to the ground; Kokālika’s body was separated from his mount; and the four legs of the elephant and horse he rode spread out upon the earth as they let out bird-like cries. They divined among themselves, saying:
"All others shall attain the Way, but these two shall meet with ill fortune."
They all went to where the Buddha was and became śramaṇas; their stubbornness was subdued, and there were none who did not joyfully accept [the teaching].
*Madhyama-āgama*, Volume Upper;
*Madhyama-āgama*, Volume Lower.
Translated by the Śramaṇa Dharmaphala of the Western Regions and Kang Mengxiang during the Later Han Dynasty. Chapter Seven: Sudatta.
The Buddha, departing from his native land together with a community of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, traveled to the Bamboo Grove in the kingdom of Rājagṛha.

The elder Boqin, receiving the Buddha’s gracious descent, hurried to the Bamboo Grove and prostrated himself five times at the Buddha’s feet. He stood respectfully with some hesitation, composed his mind, and addressed the Buddha:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will deign to accept these humble offerings of food.”
The Buddha’s silence was his consent.
The householder, filled with joy, prostrated at his feet and withdrew.
Returning home, he prepared the finest delicacies, adorned the site with banners and streamers, and personally attended to the service with flavors unsurpassed in this world.
The elder of Śrāvastī was named Sudatta (translated into Chinese as Shanyun).

Although he had not yet met his host, Boqin, they constantly communicated through letters; as their conduct was identical and their virtue equal, they regarded each other as friends from afar, exchanging salutations across the distance.
Sudatta came on business and, seeking out his relatives, went to visit them; however, his uncle was so diligently engaged in making offerings that he could not be released.
Sudatta hesitated for a very long time, then called out to the servant and said, "I have come from afar specifically to meet you in person.
My sincere heart has been with you since long ago, and I have hurried here to express my long-held feelings."
"I did not expect that today I would be so slighted and find no affinity.
After Kālaṃkāra had finished his business, he came out, bowed to him, and sat down, saying:
"In the past, when we did not meet face-to-face, you condescended to visit me; my feelings of longing and expectation have been redoubled by your arrival."
"To invite a great guest with such explicit urgency causes their heart to become stagnant and disordered.
Shanwen asked, "Who is meant by 'a great guest'?"
"Is this for a wedding, a national festival,
or a gathering? He replied,
"Fellow practitioner!..."
Have you not heard?
The Crown Prince of King Śuddhodana entered the mountains six years ago; having perfected the Way, he is now titled Buddha.
His majestic appearance is brilliant and far-reaching, and his divine spirit illuminates the hidden depths.
His body was sixteen feet tall, with a complexion like purple-gold, radiating brilliance throughout the world. He expounded the Dharma and set forth the precepts;

his refined meaning penetrated the divine. His followers were known as the Bhikṣu Saṃgha; they dwelt in stillness, rectifying their persons, cultivating virtue, and treading the Way. Spurning glory and abandoning profit, they were called "True Men" (Zhēnrén); there were one thousand two hundred and fifty of them in all.
When Shanwen heard the sound of the Buddha’s name being invoked, the hairs on his entire body stood on end and his heart rejoiced so deeply that it pressed against his chest.
He waited for dawn in a state of rapturous anticipation; his five senses were stirred within him, and he tossed and turned, unable to sleep.
His utmost sincerity moved the divine response; in the middle of the night, it suddenly became bright, and he immediately prepared to set out.
As he headed toward the city gate, he looked back toward the left side of the city and saw a shrine dedicated to a deity named Lèpī.
In the past, when he had finished his prostrations and was looking back, he suddenly fell into a deep stupor.
Shanwen was terrified and did not know where to turn; yet, despite this calamity, his mind still remained fixed on the Buddha. Because of his utmost sincerity, his fear and dread were dispelled.
A voice from the sky said: "Excellent, Sudatta!"
"The mind has reached such a state!
He then asked the voice in the air,
"Which deity are you?"
He then replied to him,
saying, "I am your kinsman, Māgandiya! He asked:
"From where were you born?
Why have you come to this place?
He immediately replied:
"In the past, I heard the Dharma from the Buddha’s disciple of supernormal powers, Mahāmaudgalyāyana.
By virtue of this meritorious retribution, I was born in the first heaven; yet my merit was very slight, and thus I have been separately appointed to preside over this place."
I see that you have come with a sincere heart to assist me.

The Buddha is the Most Honored One; even in the space between raising and lowering one's foot, his blessings and protection are immeasurable. It is my regret that during my lifetime I did not obtain the opportunity to behold the Buddha.
"What I have seen now clearly verifies the True Dharma.
The heavens emitted a great light that illuminated the Bamboo Grove.

Śāṇakavāsin followed the light and saw the Tathāgata from afar; he was even more impressed than what he had heard. He stepped forward to prostrate himself, then withdrew to stand aside. Observing the Buddha’s physical marks with a humble mind, he questioned the Buddha:
"Is the Honored One at ease?
For the sake of Sudatta, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Without the marks of sorrow or joy, The mind is empty, pure, and at peace."
Having attained the state of non-arising, one perceives the Truth and enters Nirvana.
With awakening, right mindfulness, and clarity, one has already crossed the abyss of the five realms;
the net of craving and attachment is severed and destroyed, forever stilled, joyful, and at peace.

When the elder Sudatta heard these words, by virtue of his past merit, he immediately gave rise to a pure mind and attained the Dharma-eye. He took refuge in the Triple Gem, received the five precepts, and became a lay follower (*upāsaka*).
He came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I only pray that the Tathāgata will deign to visit Śrāvastī for a time to provide instruction, thereby delivering both ruler and subjects.
The World-Honored One replied:
"What is your clan and name? The elder knelt and replied, "My humble style name is Sudatta;
because I support orphans and the elderly and provide them with food and clothing, the people of the country call me 'Givaka' (the Provider for the Lonely and Destitute)."
The Buddha asked, "Is there a vihāra there that can accommodate my assembly? They replied:
"No," replied the elder Sudatta.
Receiving the Buddha’s holy command, he stepped forward, knelt down, and addressed the World-Honored One:
"I am capable of undertaking the construction of a vihāra; I only require a bhikṣu to oversee the site."
He looked back and commanded Śāriputra to assist him in the preparations; immediately accepting the instruction, he paid his respects and withdrew.

Returning to Śrāvastī, he traveled about seeking land until he found that only the Jeta Grove was suitable—it abounded with various fruits and flowing springs, where wondrous birds gathered in flight; the ground was level and the trees lush, and it was close to the city. He went to the keeper to request [the land], but the man showed no intention at all to sell.
Seeking it without ceasing, he spoke with indignation, saying:
"If you can cover the entire garden with gold coins, only then will I come out.
He asked this again.
"Is this truly so? Jizhi replied, "The price is high;
you certainly could not afford it. I was merely joking to settle the matter!"
"What more is there to doubt?
Sudatta took his leave and returned, carrying a carriage to deliver the money.
The park superintendent would not allow it and ran to inform the master of the house:
"Su-datta has sent money; I wonder whether it has been received?
He then instructed the park keeper:
"I was merely speaking in jest; do not accept the money."
The two men disputed with one another, and the elders of the entire kingdom rushed there to intercede and stop them.
The elders adjudicated:
"The price for the land has already been settled; it should not be subject to regret."
"The administration of the state is clear and peaceful; I shall not violate the law.
He then permitted the distribution of money.
When the distribution was incomplete within the gate, Zhi joyfully said:
"I have regained my garden! he exclaimed, and dispatched men to urge its completion.
Sudatta went there in person to inspect it with him; however, his plans were not yet complete, and his mind was troubled and unhappy.
Gijjha said,
"If the wise man of the kingdom regrets it, then let it stop.
He replied, saying:
“I have no regrets.
He thought only of obtaining the hidden treasure, for he had merely leveled the ground.
Then Jeta thought to himself:

"The Buddha must be the Most Honored One, for he can cause such a man as this to exhaust his wealth without regret; he is worthy of veneration and emulation, possessing such divine and wondrous power.
He then said to Sudatta, "Do not pay any more money;
let us purchase the remaining land with trees and together establish a vihāra."
Sudatta immediately said,
"Excellent! I grant my consent."
Thereupon, they applied themselves to the task; the monastic quarters, seating mats, couches, and rugs were made as exquisite as anything in the world.

They further displayed banners and streamers, sprinkled the ground with fragrant liquids, and prepared all manner of offerings, including various delicacies and rich foods. Burning many kinds of famous incense, they knelt from afar and entreated the Buddha, saying:
"We only pray that the Tathāgata will deign to humble his divine majesty and visit us."
Thereupon, the World-Honored One, together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, traveled through the kingdom of Śrāvastī in response to the invitation of Sudatta.
The majestic spiritual power caused the earth to tremble, and all within the kingdom rejoiced; men and women, young and old, crowded the roads as they came forth.
Anāthapiṇḍada and King’s younger brother Jeta came forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and together ascended to the vihāra.
The Buddha accepted his prayer for blessings; thus, it was called the Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍika Ārāma.
When there was urgent business in the kingdom, he summoned Sudatta, who hastened to attend the assembly.
Once the matter was concluded, he returned in haste, observing the fast with the utmost reverence.
As he proceeded on foot along the road, he encountered someone carrying a jar of curd; having no one to whom he could entrust it, he took it up himself and continued on his way.
Ahead, he met a brahmin and requested him to carry it for him.
They went together to the vihāra, where [the Buddha] personally served the food.
He looked back and commanded the brahmin, "You may serve the food yourself.
When the meal was finished and they had performed the ritual washing, they listened to the Dharma with solemnity; everyone rejoiced and praised him boundlessly.
When the brahmin returned in the evening, he observed the fast and did not eat.
His wife, finding this strange, asked him:
"I wonder what you are grieving over?"
He replied, "I am not angry;
it is simply because I am observing the fast.
His wife questioned him further:
“From where have you come for the fast?
The brahmin replied, “The householder Anāthapiṇḍada has provided a meal for the Buddha in his garden and invited me to attend the fast; the fast is called the Eightfold Precepts.”
His wife shed tears and said with indignant anger, "You have destroyed the inherited norms; this calamity has now arisen!
Gautama’s subversion of the Dharma—how could it ever be worthy of acceptance?"
Being pressed and urged without ceasing, they sat down together to eat.
The Brahmin’s life span ended at midnight, and he was reborn in the kingdom of Uddiyāna as a tree spirit of a great marsh.
At that time, there were five hundred Brahmins and others who wished to go to the Triple Sacrificial Pond at the Ganges to bathe away their impurities and hope for the state of a divine immortal.

On the way, they ran out of provisions; seeing that tree from afar, they imagined there was a flowing spring beneath it and rushed toward its base, but found nothing at all. Exhausted and distressed in that marshy place, they were overcome by hunger and thirst.
A tree spirit manifested in human form and asked the brahmin,
"Where have you come from, ascetic?
Where are you going now?"
They replied in unison, "We wish to go to the Divine Pond to bathe and seek immortality; today we are hungry and thirsty, so we pray you will have compassion and aid us.
The tree deity then raised his hand, and all manner of flavors flowed forth in abundance.
When the assembly had eaten their fill,
they went to the deity and asked:
"By what merit has such a magnificent result as this been brought about?"
The deity replied to the brahmin:

"Because I observed the eightfold fast for the sake of Anāthapiṇḍada of Śrāvastī, I was thwarted by my wife and failed to complete the practice; consequently, I have been reborn in this marsh as the spirit of this tree."
"If you complete the ritual of the fast, the merit will lead you to be born in heaven.
At that time, the tree deity spoke in verse:
"Sacrificing plants sows the root of calamity; Day and night it grows its branches and twigs."
"The suffering of the present life destroys the root of the self; through the Dharma-precepts, one becomes an immortal who transcends the world.
Upon hearing this verse, the Brahmin’s delusion was dispelled and he accepted it with faith, then returned to Śrāvastī.

The route passed through a country named Kūlani. In that country there was an elder named Ghoṣila—which means "Beautiful Voice" in the Jin language—who was revered and loved by the people; whenever he spoke, they would immediately comply with his words.
A group of brahmins went there seeking lodging.
Sundarī asked them, “Sirs, from where have you come?”
"Where do you intend to go now?

[The youth] related in detail the merits of the tree deity of that marsh and expressed his desire to travel to Śrāvastī to visit the householder Ghoṣila and attend his Dharma-precepts assembly, so as to fulfill his original aspiration.
Beiyin was filled with joy; pursued by the merit of her past conduct, she immediately understood and desired to practice it. At dawn the next morning, she issued a proclamation:
"Among my kinsmen and those I hold dear, who can go together to receive the ritual for the fast?"
A total of five hundred people responded unanimously to the call; drawn by their original vows and moved by the gravity of the matter, they set forth.
They traveled toward Śrāvastī, but before reaching Jetavana, they encountered Sudatta on the road. As they were passing by on their way to the Buddha’s dwelling, they did not recognize him.
The counselor asked his attendants,
"Who is this gentleman? They replied, "He is Anāthapiṇḍika."
The assembly of brahmins rejoiced and pursued him, saying:
"Our wish is fulfilled; we have sought a person and found him.
They hurried forward to meet him and, with one voice, exclaimed:

"I have long enjoyed the reputation of your noble virtues and have gazed upon you with a humble and reverent heart. Having heard that you possess the teachings on the Eightfold Precepts of the *Guanzhai* (Eightfold Fasting), I have traveled from afar to seek refuge under your guidance; I am most fortunate to receive your instruction."

Sudatta stopped his carriage and replied, "I have a Great Master known as the Tathāgata, the Benefactor of the Multitudes; he dwells nearby at the Jetavana to deliver sentient beings. We may proceed together to visit the World-Honored One."
Having heard these instructions, they respectfully assented.

With solemnity and utmost devotion, they gazed afar at the Tathāgata; joy arose within their hearts, and they prostrated themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, then withdrew to sit to one side.
Observing their fundamental minds, he expounded the essentials of the Dharma.
Five hundred brahmins attained the stage of Anāgāmin and subsequently became śramaṇas;
Maitrakanyaka and his followers attained the Dharma-eye.
The bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying,
“How swiftly have these five hundred brahmins and the various elders attained the Way?
The World-Honored One replied:
"Not long ago, in a past age, there was a Buddha named Kāśyapa who preached the Dharma for the assembly, declaring that I would appear in the future.
Now, these brahmins before that Buddha have made a vow and aspiration to behold the future Śākyamuni Buddha."
These elders also share this same aspiration.
For this reason, upon seeing me, they immediately attain liberation.
The bhikṣus were filled with joy and received these teachings with wholehearted devotion.
The nun Sunanda thought to herself that she wished to invite the World-Honored One.
Knowing her thought, the Buddha told her:
"He has no vihāra; thus your wish shall not be fulfilled."
Gulandharā, delighted and understanding, stepped forward with joy and addressed the Buddha:
"I have a private residence; I wish to offer it as a vihāra.
I pray that you will compassionately grant me this favor, so that you may deliver all living beings."

He requested to return to his kingdom to prepare the offerings he had promised; having prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, he completed his salutations and departed. Chapter 8: The Origin of the Appearance of Kāśyapa.

At that time, the Tathāgata, together with a community of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, traveled from the Jeta Grove in Śrāvastī to the Citradhvaja monastery in the kingdom of Kuṇāla. As his foot stepped upon the threshold of the gate, heaven and earth shook; pearls and jeweled musical instruments resounded spontaneously without being struck; hidden poisons and toxins were pacified, and auspicious signs filled the air with harmony and purity.
On that day, among the people of the realm, there was none who did not pay respectful homage and look up to the World-Honored One with longing.
At that time, there was a king named Udayana, who was tyrannical and oppressive; he listened to the words of flatterers, was addicted to the music of women, and was submerged within a net of doubt.
Furthermore, he appointed two principal consorts to serve him in turn on his left and right; the beauty of these two queens was peerless within the entire kingdom.

The consort on the left, whose name was Zhàotáng, was haughty and arrogant by nature; she followed only what was evil, slandering and persecuting the virtuous and good without ever being satiated in her calumny.
The aforementioned lady was named Gai Rong; she practiced benevolence and love, was devout and reverent, lived with pure simplicity and self-restraint, and never adorned her body with finery.
The King treasured her integrity and treated her with private favor in all matters.
Zhao Tang harbored jealousy and slandered him most deeply; however, the King examined his conduct and did not accept his words.
Gaorong had an elderly attendant in blue robes named Dusheng, who constantly went to the market to purchase incense.

On his way back to pay his respects, he would pass by the monastery every time and offer his reverence; he reduced his expenditure on incense, pooling these savings together to provide meals for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, which he committed to memory without forgetting.

Having finished his almsgiving, he returned to the palace; on the way, he passed a shop and took some incense. Due to the merit of this deed and the influence of his past practices, the fragrance that reached his nostrils was twice as potent as usual.

When interrogated and his reasoning exhausted, he confessed the truth of his circumstances: he had regularly reduced his expenditure on incense to provide meals for the Buddha and the Sangha; the Dharma was profound and its meaning subtle, unlike anything heard in the world.
Upon hearing the sound of the Buddha’s voice, Gāṅgā was struck with awe and her heart filled with joy; she thought to herself:
"My heart leaps with delight; by what cause have I been able to hear such immeasurable Dharma?"
He then said to Dhaññājāni,
"Try to explain it for me. Dhaññājāni replied:
"My body is lowly and my speech is impure; I do not dare to proclaim the honored words of the Tathāgata myself.
He requested to go to the Buddha to receive his instructions and then return, whereupon [the king] sent him out from the palace.
He addressed him again, saying:
"Having fully received the ritual instructions, while you have not yet returned, the lady and her attendants are waiting anxiously in the central courtyard.
The Buddha said to Duṣvanta:
"You return and preach the Dharma; there will be many who are delivered.
As for the ritual for preaching the Dharma, first provide a high seat.
Having received this command, Du Sheng proclaimed the holy decree in full.

Gaīya was filled with joy; she opened her casket, took out her garments, and piled them to form a high seat. Sustained by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, he preached the Dharma as was appropriate.
Lady Gaīya, along with her attendants, had their doubts resolved and their afflictions destroyed, attaining the stage of *srotāpanna*.
When Du Sheng reached the appropriate time, he attained the *dhāraṇī*.
Zhao Tang harbored resentment, and jealousy and indignation arose within him; he slandered [Du Sheng] on numerous occasions.
The King, in turn, insulted him, saying:
"You wretched sorcerers, your words do not reach the realm of righteousness; that man’s conduct and adherence to principle are truly noble.
Although Zhaotang harbored resentment in his heart, he still wished to harm him.
Mimi said to the king:
"She constantly dispatches her maidservant to come and go at the Buddha's abode; her feelings are dissolute as she consorts with outsiders, and her ambitions overflow toward heterodox paths.
Although I am truly virtuous and upright, I am neglected."
As he slandered him incessantly, the king became somewhat deluded by his words.
Zhaotang plotted in his mind, thinking:
"I shall certainly succeed on the day of his fast!"
Watching for the day of the fast, he took the opportunity to advise the king, saying:
"For today's feast, you should invite the Right Consort.
The king then issued a general summons, and all those so commanded assembled.
He was permitted to observe the fast, yet alone he did not accept the summons.
Though summoned repeatedly three times, he remained steadfast in his principles without wavering.
The King’s wrath grew intense; he dispatched men to drag him out, bind him before the palace hall, and intended to execute him by archery.
The man showed no fear and with single-minded devotion took refuge in the Buddha.
When the king shot at him himself, the arrow turned back toward him; each subsequent arrow likewise returned.
At that moment, the king was greatly terrified; overcome by panic, he surrendered and asked him:
"What sorcery do you possess that has brought this about? The lady replied, "I serve only the Tathāgata and take refuge in the Triple Gem.
Each morning I observe the Buddha’s fast, abstaining from food after midday, practicing the eight precepts, and ensuring that no ornaments remain upon my person."
"It must surely be that the World-Honored One regards us with such compassion!
The King said, "Excellent!"
"How can you say it cannot be done?
You must go to the vihāra to pay your respects and manifest your devotion.

At that time, an enemy state raised an army and entered the borders; as their forces were formidable and powerful, the King personally went forth to campaign, entrusting the Brahmin named Śubhagraha with the provisional administration of the state affairs.
Zhaotang said with joy,
"Now that my father has taken over the administration, he will surely kill me.
After Wang had departed, the woman conspired with her father to burn Gai Rong and his attendants to death, falsely claiming it was an accidental fire so that they might conceal the crime.
When the matter was eventually revealed, the King became greatly incensed; he banished Jixing to the outskirts and cast him away, yet spared his life because he was a Daoist.
He imprisoned those such as Zhaotang in underground caves, suppressed the heterodox ways, and extensively propagated the Buddha-dharma.
The bhikṣus withdrew from their seats and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Queen Gaīyā and her attendants have been so diligent that they have seen the Truth and attained the Way; we wonder what transgression they committed to meet with such calamity by fire?"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will reveal what has not yet been heard.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"In the past, there was a city named Vārāṇasī. There were five hundred courtesans who attracted frivolous men to provide for their livelihood."

In the world there was a Pratyekabuddha named Kāla, who taught and transformed the people, leading them to observe the five precepts; all the men and women of the kingdom turned their hearts toward him as their teacher.
The women became indignant and said,
"Who is this man who has come to interrupt our guests?
They all rose up in anger and conspired to plot his ruin and harm.
On a later day, Kāla entered the village again; the women, all equally enraged, struck and beat him with fire-hearth stoves until his entire body was scorched and mangled, yet he felt no regret.

He then manifested his supernatural powers, soaring into the void. The women were struck with terror and wept as they repented their transgressions; kneeling for a long time with heads raised, they expressed their feelings, saying:
"We women are dull-witted and ignorant of the Ultimate Truth; a foolish and deluded multitude have brought disgrace and insult upon the Divine Spirit."
Reflecting upon my own transgressions, my sins are as vast as a mountain; I pray that you will descend with your divine virtue to extinguish these heavy calamities.
As soon as he heard these words, [the Buddha] descended and entered parinirvāṇa.
The women built stupas and made offerings to the śarīra.
The World-Honored One further said:
"Those courtesans were Gaorong and the others."
"Sin and merit follow a person; after a long time, they will inevitably manifest.

When this Dharma was preached, those of all ranks within the kingdom—both great and small—believed, submitted, and rejoiced. They all took refuge in the Triple Gem, received the precepts, and withdrew.
The Buddha and the bhikṣus returned to Śrāvastī and stayed at the Jetavana.

Chapter Nine: Mahāprajāpatī Comes Forth and Becomes a Bhikṣuṇī. At that time, the Buddha was traveling in the kingdom of Kapilavastu and was staying at the Śākya Monastery together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī went to where the Buddha was staying; she prostrated herself in salutation, withdrew to stand to one side, and with palms joined, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have heard that if women practice with diligence, they may attain the four fruits of the śramaṇa path. I pray that I may receive the Buddha’s Dharma and Vinaya."
"Because I have faith while living at home, I wish to leave the household life to practice the Way.
The Buddha said, "Stop, Gautamī!"
"There is no joy in admitting women into my Dharma and Vinaya.
Those who don the Dharma robes should, for as long as life lasts, remain pure and fully cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Thus did Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī entreat him again, even up to three times, but the Buddha would not grant her request.
He then went forward to pay his respects, circumambulated the Buddha, and departed.
Not long thereafter, the Buddha, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus, traveled from the Śākya vihāra into the kingdom of Kapilavastu.

When Mahāprajāpatī heard that the Buddha had come from among his disciples into the kingdom, her heart was filled with great joy. She immediately went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and addressed the Buddha again, saying:
"I have heard that if a woman exerts herself with diligence, she may attain the four paths of a śramaṇa; I pray that I may receive the Buddha’s Dharma and Vinaya."
"Because my household possesses faith, I wish to leave home to practice the Way.
The Buddha said, "Stop, stop!
"Gotamī! There is no pleasure in women entering my Dharma and Vinaya.
Those who don the Dharma robes should, for as long as life lasts, remain pure and fully realize the holy life."
Mahāprajāpatī then again entreated him with compassion, repeating this up to three times, but the Buddha would not grant her request.
She then came forward, paid her respects, circumambulated the Buddha, and departed.

At that time, the Buddha remained in this country with the bhikṣus for three months to avoid the rain. Once his robes were finished and mended, he put on his robes, took his bowl, and left the country.
Mahāprajāpatī, together with the elderly women, followed after the Buddha.
As the Buddha traveled on, he arrived at the district of Nādikā and halted by the riverbank.
Mahāprajāpatī then went forward, prostrated herself in salutation, and standing back, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have heard that through diligence, a woman may attain the four paths of a śramaṇa; I wish to receive the Buddha’s Dharma and Vinaya.
Since I possess faith while living as a householder, I desire to leave the home life to practice the Way."
The Buddha said, “Stop, stop! Gautamī!”
"There is no joy in allowing women to enter my Dharma and Vinaya.
Those who don the Dharma robes should, for the rest of their lives, remain pure and fully cultivate the holy life (*brahmacarya*).
Mahāprajāpatī then entreated him with compassion, repeating this request up to three times, but the Buddha was unwilling to grant her wish.
He then stepped forward to pay his respects, circumambulated the Buddha, and withdrew.
Standing outside the gate, clad in tattered rags and barefoot, his face was soiled and his garments stained with dust; his body was weary as he sighed and wept in sorrow.
Seeing his maternal aunt Mahāprajāpatī in such a state, the wise Ānanda immediately asked her:
"Gautamī! For what reason are you wearing these tattered clothes and walking barefoot, with a soiled face and dust-covered garments, exhausted and weeping?"
Mahāprajāpatī replied, "Venerable Ānanda!
It is because of women that I am now unable to receive the Buddha’s Dharma and Vinaya; for this reason, I grieve for myself!"
Ānanda said: "Stop, stop! Gautamī!"
"Furthermore, please set your mind at ease and wait while I now enter to speak of this matter before the Buddha.
The worthy Ānanda immediately entered, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, knelt with his right knee on the ground, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have heard from the Buddha that a woman who exerts herself with diligence can attain the four fruits of the śramaṇa."

Now Mahāprajāpatī, with a sincere heart, wishes to receive the laws and precepts; having already possessed faith while living as a householder, she now desires to leave home to practice the Way. We pray that the Buddha will grant her permission!
The Buddha said, "Stop, stop! Ānanda!"
I do not permit women to enter my Dharma and Vinaya to become śramaṇas.
Why is that? Ānanda!
For example, if a family of noble lineage has many daughters and few sons, one should know that such a family is considered weak and will not attain great strength and prosperity.
If women were now permitted to enter my Dharma and Vinaya, they would certainly cause the Buddha’s pure Brahma-conduct not to endure for long.
It is like a field of rice where the grain has fully ripened, yet because of the presence of foul vapors and calamitous miasmas, the wholesome crop is ruined and destroyed.
"If women are now permitted to enter my Dharma and Vinaya, it will certainly prevent the Buddha’s pure Great Way from flourishing for long.
Ānanda spoke again:
"Now, Mahāprajāpatī possesses many virtuous intentions."
"When the Buddha was first born, he nourished himself by his own power until he reached adulthood.
The Buddha said, "It is so."
Ānanda! Mahāprajāpatī has great faith and many virtuous intentions; she has been kind to me.
Seven days after I was born, my mother passed away, and it was Mahāprajāpatī who raised and nurtured me until I reached adulthood.
Now, as I am a Buddha in this world, I have likewise bestowed great kindness and virtue upon Mahāprajāpatī.

It is solely because of me that Mahāprajāpatī has been able to take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus; furthermore, she has come to believe in the Buddha, believe in the Dharma, and believe in the Saṅgha of Bhikṣus. She no longer doubts suffering, no longer doubts its origin, no longer doubts its cessation, and no longer doubts the path; thus she has perfected her faith, perfected her precepts, perfected her learning, perfected her generosity, and perfected her wisdom.
Furthermore, he is able to exercise self-restraint: he does not kill living beings, does not steal, does not engage in sexual misconduct, does not speak falsely, and does not drink intoxicants.
Thus it is, Ānanda!
Even if one were to provide clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medical care for the sick throughout their entire life, it would not equal this merit and grace of mine.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If a woman wishes to become a śramaṇī, there are eight rules of respect which she must not transgress; she should study and practice them for as long as her life lasts."
It is like protecting against water: one must skillfully repair the embankments and dikes so that there is no leakage.
Those who can act in this manner may enter my discipline and precepts.
What are the eight rules of respect?
First, when a bhikṣu maintains the great precepts, a bhikṣuṇī shall receive the true Dharma from him.
Second, when a bhikṣu-saṃgha maintains the great precepts for more than half a month, the bhikṣuṇīs shall pay them homage and serve them.
Third, monks and nuns shall not dwell together or reside in the same place.
Fourth, when staying in one location for three months, they must examine and restrain themselves; whatever they hear or see, they should reflect upon and scrutinize their own conduct.
Fifth, a bhikṣuṇī must not interrogate the bhikṣu-saṃgha regarding their affairs based on what she has heard or seen.
If the bhikṣu-saṃgha interrogates a bhikṣuṇī regarding what they have heard or seen, the bhikṣuṇī must immediately conduct a self-examination.
Sixth, if a bhikṣuṇī aspires toward the Dharma, she may inquire of the community of bhikṣus regarding matters concerning the Sūtras and Vinaya.

Seventh, if a bhikṣuṇī has not yet attained the Way and violates the precepts, she must go before the assembly every half-month to confess her transgressions and repent, thereby abandoning an attitude of arrogance.

Eighth, although a bhikṣuṇī may have been ordained for a hundred years and uphold the great precepts, she must take a seat below that of a newly ordained, junior bhikṣu and pay him homage with humility and respect.
"These are the eight rules of respect; I teach that women must not transgress them, but should study and practice them for as long as they live.
If Mahāprajāpatī can truly uphold these eight rules of respect, I shall permit her to become a śramaṇī."
The venerable Ānanda, having received the Buddha’s words, reflected upon them with deep discernment, then paid his respects and departed. He reported to Mahāprajāpatī, saying:
“Gautamī, do not grieve any longer;
you have already received the permission to leave the household and have gone forth from home to take up the precepts.”

The Buddha taught that for women who become śramaṇīs, there are eight rules of respect which must not be transgressed; they should simply study and practice them diligently throughout their entire lives.
"You must maintain your mind like water holding back a dam; you must skillfully repair the embankment so that there is no leakage.
Ānanda then explained to his maternal aunt, one by one, the eight points of respect as instructed by the Buddha.
He said,
"One who can do so may enter the Buddha's Dharma and Vinaya.
Mahāprajāpatī then spoke with joy:
"Yes, indeed, Ānanda; listen to my words.

Suppose there were a daughter of a family of the four castes who has bathed, applied perfumes, and adorned herself with fine garments. If someone, wishing to benefit her and ensure her safety and freedom from fear, were to tie together beautiful flowers, fragrances, and precious gems into a *peyala* (a jeweled ornament) and present it to that girl, would she not joyfully accept it upon her head?"
"Now, regarding these Eight Rules of Respect which the Buddha has taught and commanded, I too receive them with joy, vowing to accept them upon the crown of my head.
At that time, Mahāprajāpatī received the full precepts and became a bhikṣuṇī; she practiced the Dharma and Vinaya and subsequently attained arhatship.
Then, at another time, the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, together with several elder bhikṣuṇīs, went to visit the Venerable Ānanda and asked him: “Ānanda!
"These elder bhikṣuṇīs have all long cultivated the holy life and have already realized the Truths.
Why, then, should they be made to pay homage to the community of young bhikṣus who have only recently received full ordination?"
Ānanda said, "Wait a moment; I shall now go in and inquire.
Ānanda immediately entered, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
The Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī said:

"These elder bhikṣuṇīs have all long cultivated the pure conduct (brahmacarya) and have already realized the Truths (dṛṣṭasatya); how can they be made to pay homage to the community of young bhikṣus who have only recently received full ordination?"
The Buddha said, "Stop, stop! Ānanda!"
You must be careful with these words and not speak them.
What you know is not equal to what I know.
Had women not become śramaṇas in my Dharma, the heterodox practitioners, brahmins, and householders from outside would have spread their robes upon the ground and entreated the śramaṇas, saying:
"The wise ones possess pure precepts and noble conduct; I pray that they will walk upon this robe, so that I may long enjoy its merit.
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"
If women had not become śramaṇas in my path, all the people of the world would have loosened their hair and spread it upon the ground, entreating the śramaṇas with these words:
"Virtuous ones, you possess precepts, learning, wisdom, and conduct; please walk upon this hair so that we may long enjoy its merit."

"If women had not become śramaṇas in my path, all the people of the world would have prepared clothing, food and drink, bedding, and medicine for the sick in advance, wishing that the śramaṇas would come and take them themselves."

If women had not become śramaṇas in my path, the people of the world would have served the śramaṇas as they serve the sun and moon, as they serve the celestial deities, surpassing all other heterodox teachers and scholars.
"If women had not become śramaṇas in my path, the True Dharma of the Buddha would have flourished for a thousand years.
The Buddha spoke again to Ānanda:
"Because women have become śramaṇas, my Dharma shall decline after five hundred years."
Why is this so? Ānanda, there are five positions that a woman cannot attain.
What are these five? A woman cannot become a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha;
a woman cannot become a Wheel-Turning Sage King (Cakravartin).
A woman cannot become Śakra, the Lord of the Second Heaven, the Trāyastriṃśa;
a woman cannot become the King of the Sixth Heaven, Māra;
a woman cannot become the Brahmā King of the Seventh Heaven.
Now, these five positions can all be attained by a man. A man may attain Buddhahood throughout the world;
he may become a Wheel-Turning Sage King; he may become Śakra, Lord of the Devas; he may become a Māra Heavenly King; or he may become a Brahmā Heavenly King.
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, they all received them with joy and began to practice accordingly.

Chapter Ten: The Conversion of King Prasenajit. At that time, the Tathāgata returned to the kingdom of Śrāvastī and stayed at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a community of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
King Prasenajit thought to himself:
"The Buddha is of the Śākya clan; having left the household life to dwell in the mountains, he has attained unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment."
His majestic presence was divinely wondrous; devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits all revered him.
When he preached the Dharma for others, his words—whether introductory, intermediate, or concluding—were all excellent.
None who heard his teachings failed to rejoice; they opened the way to fortune and blocked the path to calamity, and through his words entered nirvāṇa.

He immediately prepared for departure, with his retinue in their usual order. Upon reaching the gate, he alighted from his carriage; the ministers all stepped forward together, and after bowing directly to him, they withdrew to sit and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Recently we heard that the son of the Śākyas sat upright for six years, perfected the Way, and was titled 'Buddha.'"
"Is this truly so? Is this what the world prizes?
The Buddha said to the king:
“I am truly a Buddha; the world does not falsely report this.
The King spoke again, saying: “Gautama!
"Because he calls himself a Buddha, he is not a Buddha.
The Buddha again replied to the king:
"In the distant past, there was a Buddha in that world named Dīpaṃkara."
I bestowed upon him this prediction:
"In a future age, ninety-one kalpas hence, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni.
You shall possess the thirty-two marks, the eighty minor characteristics, the eighteen unique and wondrous qualities, the ten kinds of supernatural power, and the four fearlessnesses."
"If one lacks even a single matter, one is not called a Buddha; I now possess them all.
Therefore, I am the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha."
The king, his mind bewildered by doubt, questioned him further, saying:
"Gautama is young, and the days of your study are very few. Why is this so?"

In this world there was a brahmin who cultivated the arts of water and fire; he disciplined his body with diligent austerity, never ceasing day or night. He had traversed all ninety-six paths of learning, and his years were many and his virtue profound.
The six disciples, such as Pūraṇa Kāśyapa and the others, whose fame covers the world, have yet to attain Buddhahood.
A Buddha is truly venerable!
Inferring from this, I harbor doubts and do not believe.
The Buddha said to the king:
"I shall now expound for you the True Dharma; listen well and do not harbor doubts.
The king replied:
"Excellent! The Buddha replied to the king:
"There are four things, though small, that must never be disregarded."
What are the four? First, although the crown prince is young, he shall become the rightful sovereign; he must not be treated with contempt.
Second, a small fire burns through grass, ceasing only when the grass is exhausted; it must not be treated with contempt.
Third, although a dragon’s offspring may be small, it can produce wind, rain, thunder, lightning, and thunderbolts; this must not be underestimated.

Fourth, although a practitioner of the Way may be young, they have already entered the profound and subtle wisdom of the essential path, traveling through the air to teach and transform others, delivering sentient beings from suffering; this must not be underestimated.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke in verse for the sake of the king:
“The Prince’s merit is perfected; he shall become a righteous sovereign. Because the foolish treat him with contempt, this calamity has arisen.”
It emerges precisely from the mind; it can be made heavy or light. What is obtained through past deeds follows the person like their own merit.
One should first contemplate the roots of virtue, and only then observe others; when the essentials of the Way are complete, O Great King, reflect upon this.
A small fire obtains grass, and that which it burns is limitless; even the precious Mount Sumeru arises from what is small.
When the wise observe things, they see neither small nor large: encountering a dragon, one does not avoid it, for even a small venom can harm a person.
The bhikṣu destroys evil and enters dhyāna with diligence; having perfected the Path and attained supernormal powers, he manifests transformations to deliver sentient beings.

Having seen the Truth, he is pure and stainless; having already crossed the abyss of the five realms of existence, the Buddha appears to illuminate the world and remove the sorrows and afflictions of the multitude.

Upon hearing these correct words, the King’s heavy defilements and emotional obscurations prevented him from resolving his doubts; failing to attain awakening, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, took his leave, and returned to his palace.
At that time, within the kingdom, there was a Brahmin who lived in great wealth and possessed many treasures, yet being old, he had no son.
He prayed and made offerings with all his might, yet no son was born until finally one was born.
When the boy reached the age of seven, he fell ill and passed away.
His father was consumed by grief; he could not rest in bed and ceased eating or drinking.
Hearing that the Buddha could eliminate sorrow and affliction, he immediately went to the Jeta Grove.
The Buddha asked the brahmin,
"What cause for distress do you have, that your countenance is so haggard?"
The brahmin said, "I am old and decrepit;
I have but one son who has abandoned me and passed away, leaving me in bitter and agonizing grief.
The Buddha addressed the brahmin:
"When people have affection and love, they inevitably encounter sorrow and grief.
The brahmin, his mind deluded, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"In the joy of affection and love, what sorrow and grief could there be?"
The Buddha said, “It is not so!
This was repeated up to three times, but the brahmin did not understand; he ran out of the Jeta Grove and saw two men playing dice, whereupon he thought to himself:
"This must be a wise person who can resolve my doubts," he thought,
and then asked the two men:
"Is affection for loved ones a source of joy, or is it a cause of sorrow and grief?"
He then replied to the brahmin:
"Among all the pleasures in the world, none surpasses those born of affection.
The brahmin spoke again:
"I have seen Gautama and he spoke thus to me.
The two replied, "The śramaṇa Gautama perverts the world and deludes people; be careful not to believe him."

The foolish people within the kingdom all mocked the Buddha’s words together; this report reached the King, causing his mind to become deluded. He then spoke to his consort—the consort’s name was Mallikā—saying, “Gautama is laughable;
he has turned his argument upside down and lost the principle.”
"How can there be sorrow and grief born from affection?
The lady replied, "The Buddha does not speak falsely; it is indeed as he says!"
The king spoke again, saying, "You revere Gautama, and furthermore, he is a kinsman; you simply believe in him.
The lady said to the king:
"Why do you not go yourself?
Or, if you send a wise minister, have him inquire about what we ask, so as to verify the world's delusions.
When the king heard these words, he immediately summoned his wise minister, Nāliśeṇa.
"Carry my voice and inquire after the health of Gautama, saying:
'The people of the world are deluded and ignorant, falsely transmitting your noble intent by recklessly claiming that grief and sorrow arise from affection.'"
"Finding their principles to be contradictory, I have therefore dispatched this messenger to receive your teachings and transformation.
"If the Buddha has any instructions, you must receive them with careful attention.
Having received the king’s command, the minister immediately went to the Jetavana, prostrated before the Buddha, and stood back; after a short while, he stepped forward, knelt, and said:
“King Prasenajit, having prostrated before the seat, asked of that which he did not understand, wishing for instruction and the proclamation of the true words.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata bade the minister take his seat and addressed him, saying:
“The root of affection and love is a deep current difficult to exhaust; the afflictions of sorrow and grief arise entirely from affection and love.”
He further addressed the great minister:
"I now question you; answer as you understand it.
Suppose there were a man whose parents had passed away, whose wife and children had all died, and whose wealth had been confiscated by the authorities."
"Is this man’s distress such that it can be overcome?
The minister replied,
"It is exactly as Your Majesty has instructed."
He further said to the minister:
"In ancient times, there was a man living in poverty and distress who married a daughter from a wealthy family; being indolent and lacking resourcefulness, he grew poorer day by day."
The family was in financial distress regarding provisions and intended to seize her to remarry her.
When the wife heard the family's deliberations, she told her husband:
"My family’s power is strong; they will certainly seize you. What plan should we devise?"
Hearing his wife's words, he intended to enter the chamber with her, saying:
"I now wish to die in the same place as you.
He then stabbed his wife and subsequently stabbed himself.
The Buddha told Nāliśeṇa:
"When those bound by affection kill one another, how can there be merely sorrow and grief?
Having received the Buddha’s teaching, the minister paid his respects, withdrew, and returned to the palace, where he fully proclaimed the Honored One’s intent.
The King’s mind remained unenlightened, and he continued to deride these words.
He spoke again to Māluṅkyaputta:
“Gautama, for what reason do you speak such words?”
The lady said to the king, "I wish to submit a matter; I pray that you will deign to consider it.
The king said:
"Speak then. The lady asked:
"In that region there are two districts; one is named Kāśī and the other is named Koṭalī."
If someone were to say to the king:
"Those two countries have been seized by another king," what should the king do?
The king said to his consort:
"My abundance and joy depend upon these two kingdoms.
Were such a question to arise, my heart would be filled with anxiety and distress."
The lady spoke again:
"If Prince Vīradeva or Princess Vajrā should fall ill or pass away, what would the King do?
The King replied to the lady:
"This emotion is unbearable.
The lady asked the king,
"Does this arise from the sorrow and grief born of affection?"
"I am a lowly and ugly concubine who has had the honor of serving in Your Majesty's inner chambers; if I should fall ill and die this very day, what will become of You, O King?
The King replied to Mallikā, "My mind is so clouded and distracted that my life itself may not be preserved."
The lady spoke again:
"Does this not give rise to grief and sorrow through affection?

The King’s mind was then relieved; he immediately descended from his couch, prostrated from afar toward the Jetavana, took refuge in the Triple Gem, repented and apologized for his transgressions, and for the remainder of his life and until the end of his days, he held the Honored Teachings upon his head.
Chapter Eleven: Cherishing Oneself. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, where he was teaching the Dharma to a fully assembled community of monks.

King Prasenajit, at the time when the sun had passed its zenith, passed by the place where the Buddha was; he alighted from his carriage, set aside his parasol, and with arms folded behind his back, stepped forward directly, prostrated himself upon the ground, and then withdrew to take his seat as king.
The Buddha asked the king,
"Where have you come from?
Your garments are tattered and your form is emaciated!"
The King immediately rose from his seat and, shedding tears, replied:
"The Great Lady of the State has departed this world; I have attended her funeral procession until the coffin was securely interred, and only now am I returning."

I have recently had the honor of receiving the World-Honored One’s visit to my humble kingdom. Though I am emaciated with grief, I longed to manifest this calamity; for my nature is stubborn, ignorant, and dark, and my mind was deluded by perverse sounds.
Only now do I understand that the teachings of the Most True One are clear: sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction all arise from affectionate attachment.
"I constantly reflect that these teachings of the Way are rarely heard of in the world.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the king, "Sit again."
"Listen well!
The king replied, "Yes, indeed."
The Buddha said:
"When sentient beings receive a physical form, whether they be old or young, noble or lowly, on the day their lives end, there are none whose bodies do not disperse."
It is like spring flowers, whose color does not remain fresh for long; once the fruit has formed, the flowers fall away, and when the fruit ripens, it separates from its source.
Even the precious mountain of Sumeru will crumble and decay at the end of a kalpa.
"The great ocean is deep and vast, yet it may still run dry.
Human life is precarious and fragile; the wise do not rely upon it. There is only the cultivation of virtue, diligent effort, and walking the Path.
At that time, the Buddha spoke in verse:
"Life is like fruit waiting to ripen; one constantly fears it will fall and rot.
Since all that is born possesses suffering, who can attain immortality?
Like a river flowing swiftly, it moves on and vanishes into the great ocean."
"The life of a human being is also like this: that which has departed does not return.
The Buddha told the King:

"A Cakravartin ruler governs the four realms, traveling through the air on inspection tours with his seven treasures in attendance; yet though he may live for a thousand years, he too must pass away in death."
The gods enjoy blessings where delicacies appear spontaneously; yet when their merit is exhausted, these too vanish and perish.

Monks who destroy evil, focus their minds on dhyāna, and remain unmoved by honor or profit—their will as steadfast as a mountain—even such divine sages of supernatural powers must still pass into parinirvāṇa.

The Tathāgata appears in the world, manifesting his body through skillful means and wisdom; with a vajra-like virtuous essence, he illuminates the great trichiliocosm. Circulating throughout the three realms to deliver all sentient beings, this Hero of the World endowed with the Ten Powers even manifests parinirvāṇa.
Living in this world, life does not endure for long; it is as fleeting as a flash of lightning or the wind passing through a courtyard. Noble rank and precious thrones are but like a dream!
Inferring the present from the past, there is no beginning and no end.
One revolves through the five paths; upon seeing the Truth, one returns to the Real.
As the Buddha was a king, he spoke this verse:
"As the swift current of a river flows onward and never returns, so it is with human life; that which passes away does not come back again.
Though one may live for a thousand years, one must still pass away in death. There is separation from all that is gathered together; there is no relative upon whom one can rely."
All in the world must die; there is no peace within the three realms. Though the heavens are joyful, even their blessings are lost when exhausted.
With a will as firm as the earth and virtue as heavy as a mountain, the True Person is stainless and returns to extinction in profound stillness.
"How wonderful is this karmic reward! All that was wished for has been fulfilled!
The Great Man of Supreme Tranquility has personally realized nirvāṇa.
Thereupon, King Prasenajit again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What is meant by 'loving oneself,' and what is meant by 'protecting oneself'?
The Buddha said:
"Excellent is your question!
Great King, listen attentively.
When a person is born into this world, they are a composite formed from the four great elements."
To be naturally dull-witted and habitually deluded, to engage in killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and deception, and to lack faith in the practice of the Way—this is not to love oneself.
To cultivate wholesome conduct and practice benevolence, to realize that the world is impermanent;
to believe in death and rebirth, and to direct one's heart toward the Triple Gem—this is to love oneself.
To uphold the precepts and restrain the mind, to believe so as to deepen the Way,
to maintain propriety with humility, and to practice filial piety with utmost sincerity—
such a person living in this world is one who loves themselves.

Accumulating goodness and practicing virtue, one’s person will suffer no injustice or calamity; when one’s aspirations and conduct are cultivated and luminous, the heavens provide protection. Whether male or female, when all virtuous deeds converge upon the person, weapons shall not wound them and tigers or rhinoceroses shall do them no harm. The method for self-protection lies solely in upholding the practice of the precepts.
The Buddha spoke in verse for the sake of King Prasenajit:
"When ordinary people commit evil, they cannot awaken to it themselves; Delighting in folly, they later receive the poison of suffering."
If one performs no wholesome deeds in life, one will fall into the evil realms at death; proceeding swiftly to the Avīci Hell, one arrives there with no provisions.
Those who cherish their own bodies should carefully guard what they maintain; by disciplining the mind and rectifying the person, one’s merit shall respond with rebirth in the heavens.
The person who possesses faithful conduct is praised by the sages; loving themselves in this way, they find swift liberation and no sorrow.
Evil conduct endangers the person, yet the fool deems it easy; good conduct most securely protects the person, yet the fool deems it difficult.
Believing in the Dharma and upholding the precepts, one who can practice with a wise mind is protected by the deities above; the wise find joy therein.
With benevolence and love that are not crooked, dwelling in peace and free from sorrow, one can eliminate anger and wrath, thereby escaping the abyss.
Upon hearing these words of the Dharma, the king’s ignorance was dispelled and his worldly hopes severed; he then received the five precepts.
His ministers and officials all gave rise to the aspiration for the Way, while devas, nāgas, ghosts, and spirits rejoiced and delighted in hearing it.

Chapter Twelve: Mahākāśyapa’s Initial Arrival At that time, the World-Honored One was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, preaching the Dharma for the assembly. Devas, nāgas, yakṣas, and the four classes of disciples were all present in full and solemn order.
Thereupon Mahākāśyapa, with his hair hanging loose and wearing tattered robes, first approached the Buddha.
Seeing him from afar, the World-Honored One praised him, saying:
"Welcome! Welcome!"
"Kāśyapa! [The Buddha] preemptively divided his half-seat and commanded him to sit.
Kāśyapa stepped forward, prostrated himself with his head at [the Buddha's] feet, and then withdrew to kneel, declaring:
"I am but a junior disciple of the Tathāgata; though he has offered me his seat, I dare not accept his command.
The great assembly all thought to themselves:
"What extraordinary virtue does this old man possess that the World-Honored One should offer him half of his seat?"
"This man is eminent and sagacious; only a Buddha can fully illuminate him.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata, observing the thoughts of the assembly and wishing to resolve their doubts, spoke extensively on Kāśyapa’s great conduct and his perfection in holiness.
The World-Honored One spoke again:
"I have used the four dhyānas of meditative concentration to stifle the mind; from beginning to end, there has been no diminution or loss.
The bhikṣu Kāśyapa also possesses the four dhyānas, and through these dhyānas he has attained a concentrated mind."
I embrace all beings with great kindness and loving-kindness;
Kāśyapa’s essential nature is likewise compassionate.
I deliver sentient beings through great compassion.
The Bhikṣu Kāśyapa possesses such great compassion.
I, however, delight myself in the samādhi of the four dhyānas, without distinction between day and night.
What are these four?
First is the formless samādhi; second is the immeasurable-mind samādhi; third is the pure-accumulation samādhi; fourth is the non-retrogressive samādhi.
The bhikṣu Kāśyapa also possesses this samādhi.
Originally I delighted in the six supernormal powers, and now I have attained them;
the bhikṣu Kāśyapa has also attained the six supernormal powers.

What are the six? First, the mindfulness of the four bases of spiritual power; second, fully knowing the thoughts of all people; third, clairaudience; fourth, seeing the original nature of sentient beings; fifth, knowing the destinies and conduct of sentient beings; and sixth, the exhaustion of all outflows (*āsrava*).
Now that I am fearless and uniquely honored throughout the three realms, I manifest the governance of the Dharma through four concentrations.
What are these four? First, the concentration of liberation; second, the concentration of knowledge; third, the concentration of wisdom; and fourth, the concentration of precepts.
"When name-and-form are both extinguished, the trace of Brahmā alone remains; there is no thought of sorrow or joy, and the root of birth and death is severed;
the bhikṣu Kāśyapa is also like this.
The World-Honored One spoke again:
"In the distant past, there was a noble king named Mandhātṛ.
His lofty conduct illuminated the world and his meritorious achievements moved all beings.
Śakra, the Lord of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, admiring his extraordinary virtue, immediately dispatched chariots and horses to the palace gate to welcome the king."

The king mounted the celestial chariot and suddenly ascended into the void; the Lord of Devas came out to welcome him and sat with the king, enjoying themselves to the full, and then escorted the king back to his palace.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The Lord of Devas at that time was Mahākāśyapa;
King Mandhātṛ was none other than myself."

In the past, the Lord of Devas offered me the seat of the fear of birth and death and invited me to sit alongside him; today, I repay that former merit by offering him the seat of the Unsurpassed, Right, and True Dharma-vehicle.
The Buddha recounted the events of the past, further augmenting his holy virtue to manifest the complete liberation of the bhikṣu Kāśyapa.
All present resolved their minds upon the unsurpassed, right, and true path; the fame of his Dharma teachings spread afar, and there were none who did not joyfully accept them.

Chapter Thirteen: The Chapter on the Daughter of Māṭhara. The Buddha, accompanied by twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus, departed from the kingdom of Kapilavastu; crossing the borders of the Vṛji country and delivering its people, he proceeded to Vaiśālī and arrived at the Āmrapālī grove.

In the city there was a woman named Āmrapālī; hearing that the Buddha had come to convert others, she felt immeasurable joy and immediately prepared herself to go out, accompanied by five hundred women.
The Buddha commanded the bhikṣus:
"Direct your minds and lower your heads; do not look about recklessly.
Form and desire disorder the person; only the Way can restrain them. To suppress the passions and examine the mind—this a wise person is surely capable of."
"Now there is a woman named Āmrapālī who wishes to hear the Dharma together with five hundred women; you all must each guard your pure conduct and maintain it without letting it lapse."
The bhikṣus responded with "So be it" and accepted the instruction.

Āṭavaka alighted from his carriage at the gate, placed his palms together at his heart, bowed his head forward, prostrated himself before the Buddha, and then withdrew to take his place among the women.
The World-Honored One told them: "Form does not endure long;

color does not remain fresh for long. Life passes like the wind; youth must inevitably decay. Do not rely on your physical appearance to dwell in impure conduct. The world is deluded; calamity arises from sensual desire. The diligent suffering of the three miserable realms can be shut out by the wise."
