Upon hearing the Buddha’s words, the woman’s mind was liberated and her desire ceased; she immediately resolved to attain the Way and took refuge in the Three Jewels.
Thereupon, Āṭavaka rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha:
“It is not because this woman is lowly that she has been able to receive the words of the Dharma.”
"I pray that the Tathāgata and the community of bhikṣus will deign to visit me tomorrow and accept my humble meal.
The Buddha remained silent, thereby granting his consent.
[The householder] rose, prostrated with his head at the Buddha's feet, and departed with great joy.

At that time, there were five hundred companions, sons of elders within the city, who, hearing that the Buddha had arrived to bestow his teachings and was staying at the Amra Grove, immediately set out together to go to the Buddha and listen to the Dharma.

His carriages, horses, and attire were resplendent with the five colors; he left the city and proceeded to the garden, while his attendants, carriages, and horses remained silent and orderly as prescribed by law.
Upon reaching the gate, he alighted from his carriage and advanced directly with palms joined; he prostrated himself to state his purpose, then withdrew to sit in the place designated for men.
The Buddha told the son of noble family:
"That your rank and position are honorable and magnificent, and that you enjoy happiness according to your wishes—all this is brought about by the merit and virtue of your past lives;
now that you have further encountered the Buddha, your merit and virtue increase."
The sons of the elders, filled with joy, withdrew to their seats, knelt down, and entreated the Buddha, saying:
"We humbly request Your Honor to deign to visit us tomorrow; we pray you will compassionately accept our simple vegetarian meal.
The Buddha then replied:
“I have already accepted an invitation; the Buddha does not grant a second promise.
The sons of the elders spoke to the Buddha again, saying, “We do not know who the host of the invitation is by name or clan.”
The Buddha said, "I have already accepted the invitation from Upāli; I shall go there tomorrow.
The son of the householder addressed the Buddha:
"This is a commoner; how could he be placed first?
The Buddha told the son of good family:
"The Tathāgata’s compassion is universal; it makes no distinction between the noble and the humble."
The sons of the elders prostrated themselves at the Buddha’s feet, took their leave, and returned home.
On the way, they addressed Āṭavika, saying:
“The Buddha is the Most Honored One; for the sake of all beings, he has come to transform our kingdom.”

"We shall provide food for the Buddha and the Sangha; we ought to go first. Since men are honored and women are held in lower status, you should follow behind. Be careful not to prepare the offerings yourself; that is why I have come to inform you."
The woman said to the elder’s son, “Do not use your superior power and authority to oppress the weak!
I now beg for four things; if you grant them to me, I shall not dare to precede you.”
What are the four matters?

First, I pray that my mind may preserve its goodness and not waver; second, I pray that my life may be preserved and not perish; third, I pray that my wealth and possessions may be preserved and not be extinguished; fourth, I pray that the World-Honored One will remain permanently to provide instruction and not depart for other lands.
He then said to the woman:
"A virtuous mind cannot be guaranteed, and life is likewise; this is not something I can provide.
They then spoke to one another:
"This woman is a person of merit; she has been the first to offer a meal to the Buddha.
Realizing this was extraordinary, they felt great joy.

Among them was a young man who felt ashamed that he had come out so late; he thought, "I must ensure she does not leave," and so he ordered the market supervisor to close the market and cease all trading.
Āṭavika and Ariṣṭa sent a maidservant to the market to purchase supplies, but she returned empty-handed.

Upon returning to inspect the storehouse, they found all manner of provisions fully prepared; however, they lacked firewood and charcoal, and though they went out to search for them, none could be found.
He brought out cotton cloth from the storehouse and soaked it in fragrant oil to provide for the meal preparations.
When the time arrived the next day, he sent a messenger to inform the Buddha.
The city gates were closed again, so the messenger returned and reported:
"The city gates are not open.
Knowing that this was the doing of the sons of the elders, the girl thought to herself:
"According to the law, one should send a messenger to announce the preparations for the offering; how can I gain entry?"
He then commanded the parrot,
"Go and inform the Buddha.
Having received this instruction, the parrot flew out of the house, whereupon the sons of the elders raised their bows and shot at it.
Having been sent as an envoy to invite the Buddha, he was touched by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power; the arrow was transformed into a flower, and he proceeded to the Buddha’s dwelling.
He hovered in mid-air and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“All preparations are complete; I only pray that Your Holiness will deign to come.”

At that time, as the World-Honored One, whose majestic deportment was the guide to the Dharma, stepped across the threshold of the gate, heaven and earth shook; dragons rained down to settle the dust, celestial music descended from above, and all musical instruments resounded spontaneously.
When the Buddha had finished his meal and the ritual washing of his hands was complete, he preached the Dharma for them.
The five hundred sons of elders, Āṭavaka, and the five hundred women attained the Dharma-eye; they all received the five precepts.
The Buddha, together with the community of bhikṣus, returned to the Nigaṇṭha Garden; everyone was filled with joy, and there were none who did not delight in hearing [the teaching].

Chapter Fourteen: The Chapter on the Questions and Doubts of the Nigaṇṭhas. The Buddha departed from Vaiśālī, accompanied by a community of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus and one thousand upāsakas, and proceeded to the countries of Nandanā and Pāvā.
At that time, within the kingdom, people served the six heretical teachers and were deluded by their wrong practices.
In the city there was a prominent elder named Ajātaśatru, who served the Nirgranthas with the utmost diligence.
Hearing that the Buddha had come to visit him, he went to the place where the Nirgranthas were and paid his respects as usual.
The Nirgranthas asked him,
"Have you heard that Gautama has arrived here?"
He replied, "I have heard it. The Nirgrantha said:
“You go and challenge the śramaṇa Gautama on a single point; you shall make him as if he were choking.
Pāṭaliputra said, “What is this one point that would cause him not to respond?”
He said: "You should challenge Gautama, saying:
'I have heard that the śramaṇas offer blessings for all beings to be universally satisfied;'"
"I have rashly led this great multitude to come to this land of famine, consuming the people's food;

this is of no great benefit. Vatsīputra accepted his instructions and withdrew. He immediately went to where the Buddha was, beholding His divine virtue and majestic appearance, which were radiantly brilliant. The disciples’ deportment was both reverent and dignified. With a heart leaping with devotion, he stepped forward with folded arms, performed a direct bow, withdrew to sit, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I wish to request one matter; I pray that you will grant me an explanation."
The Buddha said,
"Listen to whatever you wish to hear. Vatsiputra said:
"I have humbly heard that Gautama benefits all beings, causing them to attain peace and security.
Yet, leading a great multitude to visit this land of famine, you diminish the people's food supply; it is wasteful and of no benefit."
The Buddha told Ayivativyu:
"Since ninety-one kalpas ago, I have never heard of anyone who has encouraged others to perform meritorious deeds that resulted in loss rather than benefit."
I have heard that noble status, wealth, and happiness originate fundamentally from giving; there has never been a case where such acts were in vain or spent without a reward!

When a person practices benevolence and righteousness, they are praised and their fame spreads in the present life, and they shall attain rebirth in heaven hereafter. One should encourage the virtuous and rejoice on their behalf; thus, blessings and protection will follow them wherever they go.
He further addressed the householder:
"Wealth has eight perils that cause loss rather than benefit. What are these eight?

First, being seized by government officials; second, being plundered by thieves and bandits; third, failing to perceive the outbreak of fire; fourth, being drowned by water; fifth, having property arbitrarily confiscated by enemies or creditors; sixth, neglecting agricultural work; seventh, lacking knowledge of profitable trade; and eighth, squandering resources through gambling and reckless spending by wicked children.
These eight matters lead to extreme peril and insecurity; the eight calamities are about to arrive and cannot be restrained by human effort.

For this reason, the Tathāgata, through these causes and conditions, exhorts people to practice giving and establish themselves in the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). Thus, their foundation becomes deep, firm, and unshakable; fire, water, thieves, and bandits can no longer cause them harm. At the end of their lives, they will be reborn in heaven, where food and clothing will appear spontaneously.
The Buddha told the elder:

"These true words are of the utmost importance for transforming the world's ignorance and delusion. If one does not believe them, they will destroy their own human foundation and fall into the three miserable realms."
"If one can awaken the consciousness, transform what is heard, and alter one's conduct, so as to transfer the spirit into non-action, then one's destination will become clear.
When Ājñātakauṇḍinya heard the Buddha preach the Dharma, his mind was filled with joy and settled within; he withdrew from his seat and spoke of himself:
"My ignorance has accumulated delusions, and I did not recognize the true and correct. What I previously questioned was not in accordance with the Dharma, for it was truly not my sincere intention."
"Sent by the Nirgranthas, I failed in my mission with insolence; I pray that the Buddha will bestow his grace and forgive this transgression.
The Buddha said, "That you were able to realize this for yourself brings immeasurable merit."
The elder, filled with joy, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"My mind is shrouded in darkness and difficult to enlighten; I wish to ask about my doubts.
The Buddha said:
“Ask whatever you wish; I shall now explain each matter for you in detail.
The householder asked:

“I have humbly heard that the Tathāgata’s compassion is universal and saves all beings equally. I wonder, however, why the teachings of the Dharma appear partial and unequal, such that some attain the Way while others do not?”
"I have harbored doubts for a long time; I pray that the Honored One will dispel my ignorance.
The Buddha said, "Excellent is this question!"
Listen attentively and receive this well.
It is like a farmer who possesses two types of fields from time immemorial:
one field is high, dry, and fertile; the other field is low, damp, and poor.
During the harmonious season of spring, they exerted equal effort; they sowed seeds according to the seasonal timing and weeded out the weeds and impurities.
By autumn, when the harvest was gathered, there were vast differences in the measures of grain.
The Buddha told the elder:
"If human effort is not partial yet the harvest is unequal, it is because of the varying fertility of the soil.
When people hear my Dharma and receive, believe, and practice it, they obtain what they desire."
It is like a fertile field where the harvest is immeasurable;
these present bhikṣus, bhikṣuṇīs, upāsakas, and upāsikās are just such people!
They enter the profound at will, their supernormal powers being unimpeded; yet when people hear the words of the Way, they turn away and do not believe.
"It is like a field that is submerged and thus yields no growth; the six teachers, such as the Nigaṇṭhas, are just like this!
The World-Honored One spoke again:
"It is like a person carrying vessels to fetch water; one vessel is sound and intact, while the other is cracked and broken."
If one uses water for receiving [offerings], that which is intact remains ever full, while that which is perforated leaks away entirely.

When a person hears the teachings of the Way and practices with diligent effort, upholding the precepts without transgression and strictly restraining body and speech, they are like an intact vessel; what they receive is limitless.

When people hear the Dharma, yet do not accept or believe it, but instead slander and revile it, they lose their fundamental human nature and return to the evil realms; this is like a pierced vessel that can hold nothing.
The Buddha told the elder:

"It is through the wholesome deeds of past lives that one is able to see a Buddha. Although you are noble and powerful, if you do not believe in the Way, you are like a wild flower that falls away without forming fruit."
Vatsīputra was delighted in his heart and exclaimed, "Truly, these words move the divine; what you have spoken is most sincere.
He then resolved to attain the unsurpassed, right, and true path, received the precepts, and withdrew.

Everyone within the kingdom conceived the aspiration for the Way; the heterodox arts of the six masters were entirely abolished and discarded, while devas, humans, nāgas, and spirits proclaimed the sound of the Dharma.

**Chapter Thirteen: The Buddha Eats Horse Barley** At that time, the Buddha traveled from the country of Pāvā together with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus, returning to the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, within the borders of the kingdom of Śrāvastī, there was a district named Sūlāraṇa, where a brahmin named Ajita resided; he possessed great wisdom and clear intelligence, and his wealth was beyond compare.
He went to the home of Ānāthapiṇḍada; after concluding their discussion, he asked Sudatta, "In this capital city, is there perhaps any divine person who may be followed as a teacher?"
Sudatta replied: "Have you not heard?

A prince of the Śākya clan has left the household life to practice the Way; having realized the Way, he is called a Buddha. His physical form, color, and marks of excellence are such as have never been seen in the world."

His Dharma-precepts were refined and upright, illuminating and removing the defilements of the mind; his supernormal powers were clear and penetrating, as he understood the origins of sentient beings.

Among the devas, nāgas, and spirits, there were none who did not receive and honor him; whenever he spoke of the Dharma, its essential meaning entered the divine realm—far beyond what my mere firefly-like lamp could proclaim.
Upon hearing of the Buddha’s holy virtue, Ajātaśatru felt deep sorrow within his five senses and immediately asked:
"Is it possible to see where the Buddha is now? He replied:
"He is currently at the Jeta Grove, expounding the broad and vast mantras.

The next day, Ajita went to the Jeta Grove; upon entering the gate, he beheld the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power and radiant light. A heart of reverence arose within him, and he stepped forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, then withdrew to sit to one side.

The Buddha preached the Dharma for him; filled with joy and exultation, he immediately withdrew from his seat and invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus to grace him with their presence and transformative guidance for three months at one time.
The Buddha, through his divine insight, understood the causes and conditions of the past and silently accepted the invitation.
Having received the Buddha’s permission, Ajātaśatru took his leave and returned to his kingdom.
Thereupon, Ajita returned home and prepared offerings of the most exquisite and rare delicacies of the world.
On that day, the World-Honored One, together with a community of five hundred bhikṣus, went to Sūrpāraka.
At that time, Ajātaśatru was deluded by the celestial Māra and became addicted to the five desires:
first, precious ornaments; second, female musicians; third, food and clothing; fourth, honor and profit; and fifth, sensual lust.
He withdrew into the rear hall and issued an order to the gatekeepers:
"No guests shall be admitted for one month; regardless of their rank, let no one enter until I have given further instructions."
When the Tathāgata arrived at the gate, it was closed and he was not permitted to enter; thus, he stayed beneath a large grove of trees by the side of the house.
The Buddha addressed the community of bhikṣus:
“Since this commandery is suffering from famine and the people do not favor the Way, each of you may act as you see fit and go about for alms according to your own needs.”
Śāriputra received the command and ascended alone to the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where his daily food was provided spontaneously.
When the community of monks went on their alms round, they returned empty-handed for three days.
At that time, there was a horse trainer who offered a portion of barley gruel to the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus.
Having received the barley, Ānanda accepted it with his bowl and, moved by a sense of urgency and sorrow, thought to himself:
"The exquisite flavors of the devas and the meals provided by kings—I have always considered their tastes to be unworthy of the Honored One’s mouth."
"I have now obtained this barley, which is exceedingly coarse and poor.
How could I bear to offer such as this to the Buddha?
Taking the barley she had received, she approached an old woman and said:

“The Buddha is most honored; he is the supreme Sage who governs the Dharma. Now that you wish to provide a meal for the Buddha, I request that you cook it yourself, for the merit will be immeasurable.
Ānanda replied to his mother:
“I am currently preoccupied with urgent duties and cannot do it.”
A certain mother living nearby, hearing the praise of the Buddha’s supremacy, rushed out to seek him.
Ānanda gave her [some food], and she prepared it immediately.
After the Buddha had eaten and offered his blessing, Ānanda’s mind became bound; the Buddha wished to release it.
"The remaining rice he gave away was fragrant and delicious with a hundred flavors, unlike anything found in the world.
Ānanda, his mind having attained understanding, said:
"The wondrous virtue of the Tathāgata is inconceivable."
At that time, the World-Honored One wished to travel to the kingdom of Vaiśālī and first sent Ānanda to inform Ajātaśatru.
Having received these instructions, Ānanda immediately went to inform him.
When Ajātaśatru saw Ānanda approaching, his mind was still not yet enlightened,
so he immediately asked Ānanda, "Where is the Tathāgata now? Ānanda replied:
“The World-Honored One has been here for three months.
Having previously accepted your invitation, his word is not in vain; as this period has concluded, he bids you farewell and shall depart.”

When Ajātaśatru heard that the Buddha was about to pass away and realized he had failed to make an offering, grief and fear welled up within him simultaneously. He immediately hurried to the Buddha, prostrated himself with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and spoke of his own condition:
"Shrouded by the sins of my folly, I have violated the trust of my word."
"I pray that the Buddha, out of his great compassion, will forgive this grave offense.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"I recognize your utmost sincerity."
Ajātaśatru was delighted and stepped forward to address the Buddha, saying,
"I pray that you will remain for seven days, so that I may arrange offerings.
Since the end of the rainy season retreat had arrived, the Buddha immediately granted his consent.
At that time, Śāriputra descended from the heavens; as the festival season had already passed, he was about to proceed to the kingdom of Vaiśālī.
Ajātaśatru took the remaining offerings and scattered them all along the road, wishing for the Buddha to tread upon them as he passed by.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"This rice and grain for a meal is intended for eating; it is not proper to tread upon it with one's feet.
Having accepted his offering, the Buddha then offered a blessing, speaking in verse:
"Among the practices cultivated by non-Buddhists, diligence with fire is supreme.
Among studies that grow daily more brilliant, mastery of all meanings is supreme.
Among those to whom people look for refuge, the Cakravartin is supreme."
Of rivers, streams, and springs, the great ocean is foremost in depth;
Among the stars arrayed in the sky, the sun and moon are foremost in brilliance.
When a Buddha appears in the world, he is the supreme recipient of offerings.
Ajātaśatru’s mind was gladdened and his fetters were untied; he attained the pure Dharma-eye.
The people of the kingdom, both great and small, all gave rise to the aspiration for the Way. They came forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew with joy.
At that time, Ānanda, receiving the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, perceived the great doubts in the minds of the bhikṣus and accordingly addressed the Buddha:

"The Tathāgata is divinely wondrous; his threefold penetration shines far and wide, knowing the thoughts of sentient beings and the course of their causes and conditions. I wonder for what reason he ate barley at this one time?"
"I pray that the Buddha will enlighten and transform us, dispelling our manifold doubts.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"In the distant past, there was a great kingdom named Bandhumatī."
At that time, there was a king whose name was Bimbisāra.
The king had a crown prince named Vipaśyin, who left the household life to study the Way; having attained the Way and become a Buddha, he was still called Vipaśyin.
The marks and signs of physical excellence and majestic virtue were identical among all the Buddhas; they were accompanied by sixty-two thousand bhikṣus.

At that time, the father-king provided a meal for the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus, adorning them with banners and streamers of the world’s finest treasures; the city was thoroughly prepared, resplendent and magnificent.
At that time, there was a brahmin of pure conduct and high virtue who, accompanied by his disciples, entered the city on some business.
He asked the people around him:
"Is there some special festival?"
"It is because it has been so beautifully adorned.

The traveler replied, "The Prince Bimbisāra has attained the Way and is named Buddha; he shall come today, and this is for the sake of the King, his ministers, and the people making offerings to him!"
The Daoist replied:
"The people of the world are deeply deluded; why do they cast aside sweet delicacies to eat this man?
As for the person you describe, he ought to eat horse fodder."
The five hundred disciples praised him with one voice.
Among them was one person who admonished the teacher, saying:
"What you say, Master, is incorrect!"
"If it is as he says, this man’s virtue is so exalted that he ought to eat from the celestial kitchen.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The brahmin of noble conduct at that time was none other than myself."
The five hundred disciples are you all here now.
He who at that time exhorted the teacher was Śāriputra.
I have planted this seed, and it is only now that it has finally reached its conclusion.
He addressed the bhikṣus:
"Each of you must guard your mind and speech; be cautious and do not indulge in self-indulgence. Good and evil follow a person and will not leave them even after a long time.
You should cultivate clear conduct; by following this, you may attain the Way."
"My retribution for this has been fully settled!
The bhikṣus, having heard this sutra, rejoiced, received it with reverence, and practiced accordingly.
*Madhyama Āgama*, Scroll Lower.
